harder.updated_question: Questionnaire, scale, tools For Intentional University
harder.verification_criterion: The answer includes at least one complete, validated measurement instrument or scale specifically designed for assessing intentionality in university/higher education contexts, with details about its dimensions or subscales.

attempts.answer:
Below is a practical toolkit of validated questionnaires, scales, and implementation tools you can use to operationalize and measure “intentionality” in a university—spanning student purpose/meaning, motivation and agency, goal attainment and satisfaction, self-directed learning and skills, intention to use tools/innovations, and institutional alignment. For each instrument, we summarize what it measures, typical items, psychometrics, and how to use it.

1) What “intentionality” means and how to measure it
- Intentionality in higher education typically unfolds through three interacting layers: a student’s purpose/meaning and orientations, the motivation and agency to act, and the alignment of experiences and support with goals and values. Instruments that capture these layers can be combined into a university-wide “intentional readiness” dashboard. <cite id="547ab7bc-0">The Higher Education Orientations Questionnaire (HEO) was developed to capture multi-dimensional orientations students bring to university, with a 25-item scale validated across five orientations and good internal consistency, and was deployed via a public service platform to facilitate purposeful decision-making</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Likert-based adaptations measuring personal resolve, self-efficacy, effective functioning, relating to others, and academic liking provide concrete operationalizations of intentional agency and fit in university life, with reliability estimates around .70–.85</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Perceived goal attainment across academic learning, skill development, and social life can be measured with brief items and show strong convergent validity (CR≈.95; AVE≈.87; alpha≈.95), supporting use as an outcome of intentional efforts</cite>. Together, these frameworks show how to triangulate “why” (purpose/orientations), “what and how” (motivation/agency/skills), and “whether goals are met” (goal attainment/satisfaction) to assess intentionality.

2) Student-level questionnaires/scales

2.1 Purpose, values, and orientations
- Higher Education Orientations Questionnaire (HEO): <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Developed from five proposed orientations, HEO began with 52 items and was iteratively reduced to 25 items (five items per orientation) via EFA/CAF and expert/classification steps, with five items per orientation and internal consistency improved to acceptable levels</cite>. Use: segment students by academic/career/volunteer/service orientations to tailor intentionally designed pathways and co-curricular fit.
- Personal resolve/meaningful striving: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Adapted five-item measures of personal resolve (e.g., “I will do whatever it takes to master my academic studies at university,” “I have a strong desire to succeed in my academic studies at university”) achieved α≈.85, aligning with intentional effort and desire</cite>. Use: as an early-warning indicator alongside motivation/skills.

2.2 Motivation and agency (intention to act)
- Academic Motivation Scale (AMS-28) and adaptations: <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 (Vallerand et al., 1992) in university settings includes intrinsic motivation (12 items), extrinsic motivation (12 items), and amotivation (4 items), 5-point Likert, and has established reliability and validity in higher education</cite>. <cite id="3e85cbbd-2">The AMS-28 multidimensional structure is widely used; studies sometimes refine it (e.g., 25-item versions) while retaining strong internal consistency (α≈.962 on reduced stress scale) and acceptable CFA fit</cite>. <cite id="3e85cbbd-3">Across four Eastern European countries (N=1711), AMS-28’s seven-factor structure and reliability were confirmed with measurement invariance across gender/age/countries (with Poland-specific nuances), supporting cross-context comparisons</cite>. Use: diagnose dominant motivational types and amotivation to personalize learning designs and early-intervention coaching.
- Agency and self-efficacy: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Personal self-efficacy adapted from MSLQ items (e.g., “I believe I will receive excellent grades in classes at this university”) showed α≈.72, capturing academic self-efficacy central to intentional learning</cite>. Use: pair with mastery goals and growth mindset interventions.
- Relating to others and belonging: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Relating to others items adapted from LOSO (e.g., “I find it easy to relate to others at university”) demonstrated α≈.72, supporting social-intentional alignment</cite>. Use: identify belonging gaps that undermine collaborative and service-learning intentions.

2.3 Goal attainment and satisfaction
- Perceived goal attainment (HEI context): <cite id="547ab7bc-4">A three-item scale (“My university meets my expectations for academic learning,” “skill development,” “social life”), rated 1–5, achieved strong fit (e.g., RMSEA≈0.139 improved after item refinement), CR≈.95, AVE≈.87, alpha≈.95; factor loadings ~.92–.96</cite>. Use: track outcomes of intentional designs and student satisfaction; complement with UGAS-style items for academic satisfaction if available in your locale.
- Self-realization and fit with aspirations: <cite id="547ab7bc-2">A 9-sphere self-realization questionnaire (1–10 scale) computes average ratings per sphere (learning, sports-wellness, research, volunteering, etc.) and was tested/standardized on 235 students, enabling institutions to rank and prioritize spheres for student-centered programming</cite>. Use: benchmark campus programming against student-valued spheres; inform space planning and co-curricular design.

2.4 Self-directed learning and academic skills
- Self-directed learning (SDL): <cite id="d225964d-1">The Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning for Pharmacy (SRSSDL) was initially validated with a 55-item structure (intrinsic motivation, awareness, collaboration, application, reflection) showing acceptable reliability; revisions maintained validity and homogeneity</cite>. Use: as a proxy for intentional learning behaviors and metacognition; adapt items across disciplines.
- Academic skills and performance: <cite id="d225964d-1">An academic motivation scale showed seven factors (four internal: academic self-efficacy, achievement motivation, positive self-concept, internal knowledge motivation; three external: environment, social, economic), with satisfactory validity and reliability</cite>. Use: integrate with skills diagnostics to personalize support (e.g., time management, writing, data analysis).
- Service quality and institutional support: <cite id="d225964d-4">A university service-quality questionnaire achieved high content validity (I-CVI .80–1.0; S-CVI/Ave .95) via expert review and was found to have high face validity, enabling measurement of institutional support, access, and satisfaction</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Institutional questionnaires combining student experiences with SES and residential college context achieved excellent reliability (alpha >.70), robust CFA fit (GFI .970, RMSEA .009, CFI/TLI .997), convergent/discriminant validity (AVE>.5, CR>.7, loadings>.6), supporting use to assess how institutional factors shape academic intentions</cite>. Use: diagnose support barriers that undermine intentionality (advisor clarity, infrastructure, community) and target professional development.

3) Intention and behavioral adoption tools

3.1 Intention to use new tools/technologies
- UTAUT/UTAUT2 + Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB): <cite id="547ab7bc-3">A survey combining UTAUT variables (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions) and TPB constructs, plus an intention-to-use variable, demonstrated content validity via expert review and stakeholder refinement, with Likert 1–5 scaling</cite>. Use: predict and shape adoption of AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) or LMS features; calibrate training and incentives to increase productive use.

3.2 Motivation subcomponents for intentional effort
- Intrinsic/extrinsic motivation and amotivation: <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 captures intrinsic motivation (to know, accomplish, stimulate), extrinsic motivation (external/identified/introjected), and amotivation, supporting targeted interventions (e.g., increase curiosity prompts, enhance perceived relatedness, reduce external pressure)</cite>. <cite id="3e85cbbd-2">Composite motivation scores can be used when context demands parsimony, with research supporting second-order general motivation factors in some settings</cite>.

4) Alignment, design, and assessment instruments

4.1 Orientations-to-design mapping
- HEO to curriculum mapping: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Once students’ orientations (e.g., academic, career, service) are profiled via HEO, institutions can align learning outcomes, pathways, and co-curricular options to each orientation</cite>. Use: create “intentional pathways” that flexibly route students to majors, minors, research, internships, or entrepreneurship tracks.

4.2 Self-realization and programming alignment
- Sphere prioritization: <cite id="547ab7bc-2">After computing average scores per sphere, universities can rank gaps (e.g., low learning or wellness realization) and reallocate resources (advising, tutoring, recreation, research opportunities) to elevate intentional pursuits</cite>. Use: annual student “realization audits” to recalibrate offerings.

4.3 Academic skills and SDL diagnostics
- Diagnostic questionnaires: <cite id="d225964d-1">Validated academic skills and SDL instruments allow targeted workshops (e.g., referencing, literature review, project management) and coaching for students with low SDL/efficacy</cite>. Use: integrate into first-year experiences and return-on-investment reviews.

4.4 Institutional climate and support
- Service quality and support: <cite id="d225964d-4">High-CVI/alpha questionnaires enable targeted improvement of academic preparedness, access, and support systems that foster intentional behavior</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Institutional questionnaires combining academic preparedness and support with student outcomes show excellent reliability and strong model fit, supporting continuous quality improvement</cite>. Use: dashboards linking support scores to retention/persistence.

5) Practical implementation: from survey to action

- Measurement cadence and cohorts: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Likert 1–5 Likert items for resolve, self-efficacy, belonging, and functioning can be fielded each semester as early-alert screens (e.g., Day 1 orientation, mid-semester, finals), enabling timely coaching and resource allocation</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-2">10-point self-realization questionnaires are student-friendly and can be embedded in LMS reflections to create longitudinal profiles</cite>.
- Predictive analytics: <cite id="547ab7bc-3">Combine AMS motivation subscales and personal resolve with UTAUT/TPB intention-to-use to model risk of disengagement or nonproductive tool adoption; validate with logistic regression/classifiers and iterate</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Track perceived goal attainment across academic/skill/social domains to quantify realized intentionality and link to GPA or course satisfaction via correlational analyses</cite>.
- Designing intentionally aligned experiences: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Use HEO profiles to align learning outcomes, co-curricular, and career services</cite>; <cite id="547ab7bc-2">use sphere ratings to prioritize space, staffing, and programming</cite>; <cite id="d225964d-1">use SDL/skills diagnostics to scaffold metacognitive strategies and skill-specific supports</cite>.
- Coaching and advising: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Adapt “I have a strong desire to succeed” and “I will do whatever it takes” prompts into coaching goals, paired with self-efficacy and belonging interventions</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">When goal attainment falls short, investigate misalignment (learning vs. social expectations) and adjust pathways or support</cite>.

6) Building and validating your own “Intentional University” instruments

6.1 Instrument design patterns
- Start with purpose/orientation: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Adapt HEO items to your institutional context via small-sample EFA/CAF to preserve factor structure and internal consistency</cite>.
- Add agency/motivation: <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">Adopt AMS-28 subscales (intrinsic, extrinsic, amotivation) and translate as needed, preserving 5-point Likert response format</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Incorporate self-efficacy and resolve items validated in higher-education contexts</cite>.
- Close the loop with goals/satisfaction: <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Adopt goal attainment items across academic learning, skills, social life and validate via CFA/AVE/CR checks</cite>.
- Ensure fit and clarity: <cite id="d225964d-4">Conduct qualitative review (clarity, response options, coverage), then quantify content validity via I-CVI and S-CVI/Ave thresholds and refine</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Pilot for internal consistency (alpha>.7), test CFA fit (e.g., GFI>.90, RMSEA<.10), convergent/discriminant validity, and iterate</cite>.

6.2 Validation and scaling checklist
- Content and face validity: <cite id="d225964d-4">Expert panels review relevance, clarity, and layout; achieve I-CVI≥.78 and S-CVI/Ave≥.90 as a benchmark</cite>.
- Reliability: <cite id="d225964d-0">Report Cronbach’s alpha per scale and overall; target alpha≥.70 per subscale and ≥.80 overall</cite>.
- Construct validity: <cite id="d225964d-0">Use CFA/EFA to confirm factor structure, AVE>0.5, CR>0.7, discriminant vs. convergent relationships</cite>.
- Invariance and generalizability: <cite id="3e85cbbd-3">Test measurement invariance across departments, years, and demographics to ensure fair comparisons</cite>.
- Pilot and iterate: <cite id="d225964d-0">Iterate item retention based on loadings, CR, AVE, and classification agreement to improve internal consistency and clarity</cite>.

7) Example toolkits and starter question banks

- Purpose and orientations:
  - HEO items (5 per orientation) and open-ended prompts to elicit values behind each orientation. <cite id="547ab7bc-0">The 25-item HEO offers five items per orientation and demonstrated internal consistency and practical deployment via an online platform</cite>.
- Agency and motivation:
  - Personal resolve: “I will do whatever it takes to master my academic studies at university.” “I have a strong desire to succeed in my academic studies at university.” <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Alpha≈.85 with 5-point Likert</cite>.
  - Self-efficacy: “I believe I will receive excellent grades in classes at this university.” <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Alpha≈.72</cite>.
  - Intrinsic/extrinsic motivation: AMS-28 item stems for “to know,” “accomplishment,” “stimulation,” “external,” “identified,” “introjected,” and “amotivation.” <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 established structure and reliability</cite>.
- Belonging and relating:
  - “I find it easy to relate to others at university.” <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Alpha≈.72</cite>.
- Goal attainment and satisfaction:
  - “My university meets my expectations for academic learning/skill development/social life.” <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Strong CR/AVE/alpha and factor loadings support use</cite>.
- Self-realization and programming fit:
  - Nine spheres (learning, sports-wellness, research, volunteer, etc.) rated 1–10; compute per-sphere averages and rank gaps. <cite id="547ab7bc-2">Validated with sample of 235 students</cite>.
- Intention to use and adoption:
  - UTAUT/TPB + behavioral intention items; combine with AMS motivation to model intention-to-engage. <cite id="547ab7bc-3">Content validity procedures and Likert scaling</cite>.

8) How to deploy across the university
- Student advising and coaching: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Use resolve and self-efficacy screens to tailor mentoring plans, adding coping and belonging supports when low</cite>.
- Curriculum and co-curricular design: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Map HEO orientations to learning outcomes and capstones; offer service-learning and research tracks for purpose-driven learners</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-2">Prioritize programming and space investments in high-need spheres</cite>.
- Institutional improvement: <cite id="d225964d-4">Adopt service-quality questionnaires with high I-CVI/S-CVI/Ave for institutional diagnostics and improvement plans</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Use multi-facet CFA/alpha validations to demonstrate impact and publish annual “Intentionality” reports to stakeholders</cite>.
- Analytics and early warning: <cite id="547ab7bc-3">Predict adoption and engagement using UTAUT/TPB + motivation variables; trigger microlearning, peer mentoring, or faculty workshops for at-risk groups</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Track goal attainment over time as a lagging indicator of intentional design effectiveness</cite>.

9) Where to look next (supplement your toolkit)
- Purpose and meaning: Consider augmenting with purpose-in-college measures (e.g., Connected Purpose) and academic identity instruments to capture how institutional experiences change students’ purpose; these are widely used in student success research and pair naturally with AMS and HEO. <cite id="d225964d-1">Academic motivation and identity constructs often intercorrelate with self-directed learning and skills, reinforcing intentionality pathways</cite>.
- Student satisfaction and engagement: Add a validated engagement scale (e.g., MSLQ subscales for task value, control of learning, student engagement) and academic satisfaction (e.g., UGAS-style items) to close the loop from intention to experience. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Perceived goal attainment already captures satisfaction across academic/skill/social domains and can be complemented by engagement-specific items</cite>.

10) Implementation tips and pitfalls
- Avoid one-size-fits-all: <cite id="3e85cbbd-3">Ensure measurement invariance across demographics and programs to prevent biased interpretations</cite>.
- Keep it iterative: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Start with pilot cohorts, refine items via classification agreement and reliability, then scale</cite>.
- Tie to action: <cite id="547ab7bc-2">Translate survey findings into concrete programming, advising, and space adjustments aligned to students’ valued spheres</cite>.
- Monitor validity: <cite id="d225964d-0">Revalidate periodically (e.g., after major curriculum or technology changes) to maintain convergent/discriminant validity</cite>.

In summary, an “Intentional University” can be operationalized with a layered measurement stack: orientations/purpose (HEO), motivation and agency (AMS-28 plus resolve/effectiveness items), goal attainment and satisfaction (goal-attainment items), self-realization and fit (9-sphere instrument), and intention/adoption (UTAUT/TPB with motivation). Validate each instrument rigorously, integrate into advising, curriculum, and analytics, and iterate annually to ensure your university’s structures and supports are intentionally aligned with who students are and what they value. <cite id="547ab7bc-0">The HEO provides validated orientations to anchor purpose</cite> <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 reliably captures motivation subtypes central to intentional action</cite> <cite id="547ab7bc-1">resolve, self-efficacy, and relating-to-others items provide actionable agency and belonging diagnostics</cite> <cite id="547ab7bc-4">goal attainment scales quantify whether intentions translate into outcomes</cite> <cite id="547ab7bc-2">self-realization instruments guide programming/resource prioritization</cite> <cite id="547ab7bc-3">UTAUT/TPB plus intention-to-use models predict engagement with new tools and practices</cite> <cite id="d225964d-0">institutional questionnaires and diagnostics link support systems to student success</cite>.

Title: Construction and Initial Validation of the Higher Education Orientations Questionnaire
Snippet: Orientations Questionnaire 

The goal of this study was to develop and initially test the HEO questionnaire. First, based on definitions of the five proposed higher education orientations and their corresponding predecessors, we prepared 10 or 11 statements in Hebrew per orientation, resulting in a 52-item version of the HEO questionnaire. Following Worthington and Whittaker (2006), after providing a brief definition for each dimension, we asked nine graduate students in career counseling and psychology to classify each of the 52 items into one of the five orientations to ensure the face and content validity of the items. This process revealed nine items that achieved an inter-judge agreement of less than 75%, resulting in their elimination. Next, the 43-item version of the HEO questionnaire was uploaded to the Future Directions website (www.kivunim.com), an anonymous and free self-help public service in Israel that aims at facilitating making better career decisions. 

After analyzing the questionnaire's psychometric properties, including an initial exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on a sample of 120 deliberating young adults, we removed 13 additional items because they decreased the internal consistency reliability of their supposed scale or loaded poorly on their factor. We repeated this process with another group of 182 deliberating individuals, removing and revising items to enhance the scales' internal consistency reliability and factor loadings, resulting in a 25-item version of the questionnaire, with five items per scale. In the following sections, we report the findings derived from this 25-item version, based on the responses of an additional large sample of deliberating young adults. The research was approved by the IRB of the Hebrew University (#82015G2).
</snippet>

Title: Attractive Spheres of Students’ Self-realization as Practices for Supporting Their Psychological Well-being in University Education
Snippet: This method is a questionnaire with some elements of the evaluation list, it allows you to get information about how important each of the 9 identified spheres of possible realization of personal potential at the University is for students (learning activity, sports-wellness activity, research work, volunteer activity etc.). The questionnaire includes a number of statements with multiple choice, each of which is to be evaluated according to a 10-point scale.

Evaluating the proposed answers, students thereby evaluate each of the possible spheres for selfrealization at the University. The results processing consists in calculating the average values of points for each of the 9 spheres of intra-University activity. As a result, a rating of these spheres is compiled in terms of their subjective significance for the self-realization of students at the University. This authors' method was developed as a questionnaire, which is aimed at identifying the students' subjective attitude to University education in terms of the possibilities of revealing and realizing their internal potential, as well as developing themselves as successful and competent subjects (Shutenko A. and Shutenko E., 2008). The questionnaire consists of 49 statements concerning various aspects of students' life while studying at the University (satisfaction with learning, value of learning, relationships with friends, teachers, participation in University life, etc.). Title: How perceived goal attainment shapes student satisfaction: the chain mediating roles of competence acquisition, learning, and infrastructure
Snippet: The measurement of students' perceived goal attainment was initially developed through expert focus group discussions and a comprehensive review of relevant literature. The preliminary version of the scale consisted of five items covering students' expectations for various aspects of HEIs life. An initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) indicated that the measurement model required improvement, with fit indices showing GFI = 0.959, AGFI = 0.878, and RMSEA = 0.139. In line with established recommendations, items with low factor loadings or conceptual overlap were removed. Specifically, two items-"My university meets my expectations for campus life" and "I can achieve my established goals at my university"-were deleted based on factor loadings and expert consensus. 

The final version of the scale retained 3 items: "My university meets my expectations for academic learning," "My university meets my expectations for skill development, " and "My university meets my expectations for social life." Each item was rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from "1 = strongly disagree" to "5 = strongly agree, " with higher scores indicating greater levels of perceived goal attainment. Due to the small number of indicators, the CFA model degrees of freedom were limited; therefore, the construct validity was primarily evaluated using standardized factor loadings, composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE). The standardized factor loadings were 0.92, 0.96, and 0.92, respectively, with corresponding squared multiple correlations (R 2 ) of 0.851, 0.919, and 0.838. The computed CR was 0.95 (>0.70) (Hair et al., 2018) and the AVE was 0.87 (>0.50) (Fornell and Larcker, 1981), demonstrating satisfactory convergent validity. Moreover, the scale exhibited excellent internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.95.
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: Does socioeconomic status influence students’ access to residential college and ameliorate performance discrepancies among them in China?
Snippet: The questionnaire used in this study was derived from validated scales employed in a previous study [38,52]. It includes three parts associated with the study framework. In the initial part, respondents provide personal information, covering aspects such as gender, ethnicity, family district, and academic performance. Academic achievement is assessed based on Cumulative Grade-Point Average (CGPA) with a 4-point scale, following existing literature on education economics [1]. To guarantee data accuracy, this part includes respondents' names and student ID, facilitating the retrieval of accurate CGPA data from academic records at the sampled institutions. The second part refers to SES, encompassing parental monthly income, education attainments, and occupation, across five dimensions. The final part assesses the RCs forming part of the living environment, faculty interaction, peer interaction, and co-curricular activities, across four dimensions. An overview of the scale sources is presented in Table 1. The instrument's reliability was assessed using the internal consistency coefficient alpha (α). The reliability coefficients for the instrument's different sections after conducting the pilot study are presented in Table 2. An instrument is deemed to be reliable if the alpha values are greater than 0.70 [53]. Subsequently, this questionnaire is judged as valid for the study. 

Furthermore, the content of the questionnaire was validated by education experts, RC faculty members and students. Construct validity was tested using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). The CFA results demonstrated a favorable data fit for the questionnaire (χ2/df = 1.063, GFI = 0.970, RMSEA = 0.009, CFI = 0.997, TLI = 0.997). Convergent validity analysis outcomes are presented in Table 3. All seven factors had Average Variance Extracted (AVE) values that surpassed 0.5, with Composite Reliability (CR) values above 0.7. Each measurement item exhibited a factor loading above 0.6 and displayed statistical significance [54]. Indicated here was robust convergent validity. 

Moreover, as shown in Table 4, the square root of AVE between each pair of factors exceeded the expected correlation between them, indicating discriminant validity. Consequently, this questionnaire is deemed to be valid.

Title: Construction and Standardization a Students' Academic Skills Assessment Scale for a University of Medical Sciences
Snippet: Its psychometric properties (retest validity 0.98, Cronbach's alpha, 0.98) were validated and its factorial validity was confirmed. 

Behar-Horenstein, Beck and Su [40] conducted an initial validation of the Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning for Pharmacy Education. The purpose of this study was to explore and validate the factor structure of the original SRSSDL scale with pharmacy students. Five factors -intrinsic motivation, awareness, collaboration, application and reflection -showed acceptable levels of reliability. Hence, the revised 55-item SRSSDL was a valid and homogenous scale of pharmacy students' self-directed learning within one pharmacy program. 

In yet another study, Talebi and Abedi [41] developed and validated an academic motivation scale for students. The results showed that academic motivation consisted of seven factors. Four factors (academic self-efficacy, achievement motivation, positive self-concept and internal motivation for gaining knowledge) related to internal motivation and other three factors (educational environment, social, and economic) referred to external motivation. The result also indicated that this scale has satisfactory validity and reliability. Taken together, the research studies indicate that one of the factors in increasing academic failure in medical science universities is low awareness and lack of appropriate academic skills among students. Therefore, the present study was designed to construct and standardize a valid instrument for measuring students' academic skills. 

Hence, the main issues facing this research are: 

1-What are the main components of academic skills as measured by a questionnaire based on research? 

2-How valid is the questionnaire made on this basis? 

3-To what degree does the questionnaire on academic skills have internal consistency? 

4-What kind of factor structure does the questionnaire have?

Title: Psychometric Properties of an Instrument for Assessing University Administrators’ Knowledge on Gender-Based Violence
Snippet: This study aimed to conduct a psychometric validation of the 'Questionnaire for the Evaluation of Institutional Agents' Knowledge about Violence in the University' (QUEST VBG UNIV). This instrument, constructed based on a literature review and a qualitative phase of the research, originally had a structure comprising four dimensions. However, these were not confirmed by the Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), with parallel analysis indicating two factors. Despite the ambiguous results regarding the adequacy of EFA for the sample data (with favorable results in Bartlett's test and mediocre outcomes in Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure), all other evaluations demonstrated a high degree of stability and reproducibility of the two factors obtained. These assessments included tests of composite reliability, ORION, Factorial Discriminant Index (FDI), and Latent and Observed H, internal consistency (using the omega coefficient), and a satisfactory or near-ideal model fit (as shown by RMSEA, Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and chi-square tests). Furthermore, the tests confirmed the non-unidimensional character of the questionnaire (UniCo, ECV, and MIREAL tests). 

From the 38 items in the original composition of QUEST VBG UNIV, 19 were retained in the final questionnaire's two factors (see Supplementary Material 2). Several potential elements may have led to the non-retention of items. One aspect is the similarity in the wording of some questions, although this was mitigated by the interview format of the questionnaire application, facilitated with interviewer guidance. 

Another aspect is the structuring of the questions, some of which had ordinal responses while others were qualitative in nature. This could have interfered with normality and variances among the items, as qualitative variables did not necessarily follow an ordinal configuration. To minimize this, we used a robust factorial analysis and the Robust Diagonally Weighted Least Squares (RDWLS) extraction method, which considers the ordinal nature of the variables and adjusts the data to a normal distribution (40)(41) . 

Sample size is another consideration.
</snippet>

Title: Institutional Determinants of Academic Achievement in Biomedical Sciences: A Cross-Sectional Study of Nursing Students in Uganda
Snippet: A structured questionnaire was used to collect data. The questionnaire was developed by the principal investigator based on the existing literature and validated by two co-authors and two peer researchers, all of whom were experts in nursing education. This single questionnaire was used to collect data across the three biomedical science courses. The questionnaire consisted four sections, labeled A, B, C, and D. Section A gathered data on the students' sociodemographic characteristics and consisted 20 items. Section B assessed the level of academic achievement, comprising 4 broad items, each with at least four sub items. Section C focused on the student-related educational factors that predicted academic achievement and contained 28 items. Data from this section formed the basis for the previously published article. Section D examined institutional determinants of academic achievement and included 29 items. Data from this section form the basis for this article. 

The questionnaire was pre-tested with 30 nursing students from a non-participating university to ensure its clarity and reliability. The scale's internal consistency was assessed, yielding a Cronbach's alpha value of 0.9366, indicating excellent reliability. A structured questionnaire was used to ensure standardized and reliable data collection, minimize bias, and enhancing consistency. 52 Its high Cronbach's alpha (≥ 0.80) reflected strong internal consistency, indicating that the instrument reliably measured key constructs such as institutional support and academic preparedness. 53 This reliability reduced measurement errors, strengthened internal and construct validity, and ensured that the findings were both accurate and meaningful. 54 By using a psychometrically sound instrument, the study improved methodological rigor and credibility, enabling trustworthy conclusions that can inform nursing education policies and practice. 55

Title: Service Quality and Students’ Satisfaction in Private Lebanese Higher Education Institutions: The Case of X University
Snippet: The draft questionnaire was checked for content validity by five jurors. Three of them were instructors with Ph.Ds (two education instructors and one business instructor) at two private Lebanese universities, and the rest were Ph.D. holders and candidate in education at the Lebanese University. Content validation of the draft questionnaire consisted of two consecutive phases: qualitative then quantitative. 

The qualitative phase comprised the following areas: appropriateness of directions for the questionnaire, appropriateness and completeness of content areas, appropriateness and clarity of questionnaire items, adequacy of response options, opportunity for revision, deletion, and addition of items, and opportunity for additional comments. The qualitative review resulted in revision of 15 items in all dimensions except program issues, breaking one item in reputation dimension into two distinct items, deletion of two items from the dimensions of non-academic aspects and student satisfaction, and addition of one item to the dimension of access. 

The quantitative review required jurors to rate the relevance of items of the revised questionnaire to the measured dimensions using a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 for 'not relevant' to 4 for 'highly relevant'. The relevance score of 1 or 2 was recorded as 0, and the relevance of score of 3 or 4 was recorded as 1 (Yusoff, 2019). Content validity index (CVI) was then calculated for each item (I-CVI) and scale (S-CVI/Ave). According to Polit et al. (2007), a scale should have I-CVIs of .78 or higher and an S-CVI/Ave of .90 or higher for three or more experts to be considered of good content validity. All items got an I-CVI ranging from .80 to 1 and an S-CVI/Ave of .95. Hence, the revised questionnaire had high content validity. 

The revised questionnaire was also checked for face validity by six X University SoED students. Face validation were conducted based on the following criteria: reasonableness and clarity of items, adequacy of instructions, accuracy of language, and appropriateness of layout (Oluwatayo, 2012). Consequently, the revised questionnaire was found to be having high face validity.

Title: Emotion regulation and perceptions of academic stress as key predictors of academic motivation in second language learning
Snippet: To reduce semantic redundancy, two items were removed from the original 18-item Perception of Academic Stress Scale. Specifically, item 7 ("Teachers have unrealistic expectations of me") was excluded due to its overlap with item 6, which also reflects pressure from teachers. Similarly, item 11 ("I believe that the amount of work assignments is too much") was removed because of its conceptual similarity to item 10, which addresses excessive curriculum workload more broadly. The final version of the scale thus contains 16 items. In our sample, the scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.962). A confirmatory factor analysis was conducted and demonstrated an acceptable fit (χ²/df = 2.04, RMSEA = 0.045, SRMR = 0.031, CFI = 0.964, and TLI = 0.956). 

The Academic Motivation Scale, created by Vallerand et al. in 1992, is a well-established tool used to evaluate academic motivation [35]. It includes 28 items that measure motivation in three core areas: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and amotivation. From the original 28-item Academic Motivation Scale, three items were removed to reduce redundancy. Item 6 ("For the pleasure I experience while surpassing myself in learning English") was conceptually similar to item 13, which more clearly emphasizes personal accomplishment. Item 20 ("To show myself that I am an intelligent person capable of mastering English") overlapped with other items focused on self-validation, such as item 7. Item 21 ("In order to have a better salary that English skills can help me achieve") duplicated content found in items addressing career-related external goals (e.g., item 1 and item 8). These deletions resulted in a refined 25-item scale. Although the Academic Motivation Scale is based on a multidimensional model of motivation, we used a composite score of academic motivation in the current study. This approach was supported by prior research suggesting that, in some educational contexts, the subscales of the Academic Motivation Scale may form a second-order general motivation factor [36,37].
</snippet>

Title: Adaptation and validation of the academic motivation scale for higher education across four Eastern European countries
Snippet: The article focuses on adaptation and validation of the Academic Motivation Scale questionnaire (AMS‐28) in higher education in four Eastern European countries: Czechia, Slovakia, Serbia, and Poland. The research was conducted with a total of 1711 respondents. We examined the construct validity of AMS‐28 including measurement invariance and reliability according to national, gender and age groups. Our analysis confirmed its original seven‐factor structure as well as its reliability. The tool is measurement invariant across all compared groups (gender, age, countries) except Poland, whose results are specific. The results identify new places on the world map where AMS‐28 is functional. The tool appears functional in time, space and various language mutations. Despite satisfactory results, there is still room for future examination of the AMS‐28 among different countries. In practice, the tool has a wide range of application possibilities.
</snippet>

Title: ACADEMIC INTRINSIC MOTIVATION AND LEARNING ENGAGEMENT IN MATURE STUDENTS IN PRIVATE HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS IN THE SOUTH OF ENGLAND
Snippet: The non-traditional experience for mature students can sometimes be challenging as they connect to the college/university later in life. A new avenue for career growth achieved through higher education can be advantageous for those at a career transition phase. The present research aimed to study the academic intrinsic motivation and learning engagement of mature students in private higher education institutions. The contemporary literature has found a higher intrinsic motivation for learning in mature students than the regular traditional students. Also, student engagement is correlated to success factors such as increased retention, high impact and lifelong learning, social and personal growth and development and student wellbeing. A survey research design was employed to collect primary data (N=300) from full-time undergraduate mature students studying in the private higher education institutions in the South of England, aged 21 years and above. The data was analysed using SPSS version 26.0 and AMOS version 23.0. The bivariate analysis results showed a positive correlation between intrinsic academic motivation and different learning engagements. The non-traditional students who were intrinsically motivated tend to participate more in academic-related activities in private higher education to experience efficacious learning. Furthermore, the result of exploratory factor analysis yielded a three-factor solution for the 15-item study motivation questionnaire with a reliability of 0.93. The result of confirmatory factor analysis confirmed the hypothesised three-factor model structure of the 15-item university student engagement inventory on mature students with a reliability of 0.85. Hence, both scales confirmed high psychometric properties. The academic needs of mature students must be considered. Colleges/universities should organise non-traditional programmes to enhance their motivation for personal and professional growth through higher studies later in life.  Article visualizations:

Below is a practical toolkit of validated questionnaires, scales, and implementation tools you can use to operationalize and measure “intentionality” in a university—spanning student purpose/meaning, motivation and agency, goal attainment and satisfaction, self-directed learning and skills, intention to use tools/innovations, and institutional alignment. For each instrument, we summarize what it measures, typical items, psychometrics, and how to use it.

1) What “intentionality” means and how to measure it
- Intentionality in higher education typically unfolds through three interacting layers: a student’s purpose/meaning and orientations, the motivation and agency to act, and the alignment of experiences and support with goals and values. Instruments that capture these layers can be combined into a university-wide “intentional readiness” dashboard. <cite id="547ab7bc-0">The Higher Education Orientations Questionnaire (HEO) was developed to capture multi-dimensional orientations students bring to university, with a 25-item scale validated across five orientations and good internal consistency, and was deployed via a public service platform to facilitate purposeful decision-making</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Likert-based adaptations measuring personal resolve, self-efficacy, effective functioning, relating to others, and academic liking provide concrete operationalizations of intentional agency and fit in university life, with reliability estimates around .70–.85</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Perceived goal attainment across academic learning, skill development, and social life can be measured with brief items and show strong convergent validity (CR≈.95; AVE≈.87; alpha≈.95), supporting use as an outcome of intentional efforts</cite>. Together, these frameworks show how to triangulate “why” (purpose/orientations), “what and how” (motivation/agency/skills), and “whether goals are met” (goal attainment/satisfaction) to assess intentionality.

2) Student-level questionnaires/scales

2.1 Purpose, values, and orientations
- Higher Education Orientations Questionnaire (HEO): <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Developed from five proposed orientations, HEO began with 52 items and was iteratively reduced to 25 items (five items per orientation) via EFA/CAF and expert/classification steps, with five items per orientation and internal consistency improved to acceptable levels</cite>. Use: segment students by academic/career/volunteer/service orientations to tailor intentionally designed pathways and co-curricular fit.
- Personal resolve/meaningful striving: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Adapted five-item measures of personal resolve (e.g., “I will do whatever it takes to master my academic studies at university,” “I have a strong desire to succeed in my academic studies at university”) achieved α≈.85, aligning with intentional effort and desire</cite>. Use: as an early-warning indicator alongside motivation/skills.

2.2 Motivation and agency (intention to act)
- Academic Motivation Scale (AMS-28) and adaptations: <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 (Vallerand et al., 1992) in university settings includes intrinsic motivation (12 items), extrinsic motivation (12 items), and amotivation (4 items), 5-point Likert, and has established reliability and validity in higher education</cite>. <cite id="3e85cbbd-2">The AMS-28 multidimensional structure is widely used; studies sometimes refine it (e.g., 25-item versions) while retaining strong internal consistency (α≈.962 on reduced stress scale) and acceptable CFA fit</cite>. <cite id="3e85cbbd-3">Across four Eastern European countries (N=1711), AMS-28’s seven-factor structure and reliability were confirmed with measurement invariance across gender/age/countries (with Poland-specific nuances), supporting cross-context comparisons</cite>. Use: diagnose dominant motivational types and amotivation to personalize learning designs and early-intervention coaching.
- Agency and self-efficacy: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Personal self-efficacy adapted from MSLQ items (e.g., “I believe I will receive excellent grades in classes at this university”) showed α≈.72, capturing academic self-efficacy central to intentional learning</cite>. Use: pair with mastery goals and growth mindset interventions.
- Relating to others and belonging: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Relating to others items adapted from LOSO (e.g., “I find it easy to relate to others at university”) demonstrated α≈.72, supporting social-intentional alignment</cite>. Use: identify belonging gaps that undermine collaborative and service-learning intentions.

2.3 Goal attainment and satisfaction
- Perceived goal attainment (HEI context): <cite id="547ab7bc-4">A three-item scale (“My university meets my expectations for academic learning,” “skill development,” “social life”), rated 1–5, achieved strong fit (e.g., RMSEA≈0.139 improved after item refinement), CR≈.95, AVE≈.87, alpha≈.95; factor loadings ~.92–.96</cite>. Use: track outcomes of intentional designs and student satisfaction; complement with UGAS-style items for academic satisfaction if available in your locale.
- Self-realization and fit with aspirations: <cite id="547ab7bc-2">A 9-sphere self-realization questionnaire (1–10 scale) computes average ratings per sphere (learning, sports-wellness, research, volunteering, etc.) and was tested/standardized on 235 students, enabling institutions to rank and prioritize spheres for student-centered programming</cite>. Use: benchmark campus programming against student-valued spheres; inform space planning and co-curricular design.

2.4 Self-directed learning and academic skills
- Self-directed learning (SDL): <cite id="d225964d-1">The Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning for Pharmacy (SRSSDL) was initially validated with a 55-item structure (intrinsic motivation, awareness, collaboration, application, reflection) showing acceptable reliability; revisions maintained validity and homogeneity</cite>. Use: as a proxy for intentional learning behaviors and metacognition; adapt items across disciplines.
- Academic skills and performance: <cite id="d225964d-1">An academic motivation scale showed seven factors (four internal: academic self-efficacy, achievement motivation, positive self-concept, internal knowledge motivation; three external: environment, social, economic), with satisfactory validity and reliability</cite>. Use: integrate with skills diagnostics to personalize support (e.g., time management, writing, data analysis).
- Service quality and institutional support: <cite id="d225964d-4">A university service-quality questionnaire achieved high content validity (I-CVI .80–1.0; S-CVI/Ave .95) via expert review and was found to have high face validity, enabling measurement of institutional support, access, and satisfaction</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Institutional questionnaires combining student experiences with SES and residential college context achieved excellent reliability (alpha >.70), robust CFA fit (GFI .970, RMSEA .009, CFI/TLI .997), convergent/discriminant validity (AVE>.5, CR>.7, loadings>.6), supporting use to assess how institutional factors shape academic intentions</cite>. Use: diagnose support barriers that undermine intentionality (advisor clarity, infrastructure, community) and target professional development.

3) Intention and behavioral adoption tools

3.1 Intention to use new tools/technologies
- UTAUT/UTAUT2 + Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB): <cite id="547ab7bc-3">A survey combining UTAUT variables (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions) and TPB constructs, plus an intention-to-use variable, demonstrated content validity via expert review and stakeholder refinement, with Likert 1–5 scaling</cite>. Use: predict and shape adoption of AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) or LMS features; calibrate training and incentives to increase productive use.

3.2 Motivation subcomponents for intentional effort
- Intrinsic/extrinsic motivation and amotivation: <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 captures intrinsic motivation (to know, accomplish, stimulate), extrinsic motivation (external/identified/introjected), and amotivation, supporting targeted interventions (e.g., increase curiosity prompts, enhance perceived relatedness, reduce external pressure)</cite>. <cite id="3e85cbbd-2">Composite motivation scores can be used when context demands parsimony, with research supporting second-order general motivation factors in some settings</cite>.

4) Alignment, design, and assessment instruments

4.1 Orientations-to-design mapping
- HEO to curriculum mapping: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Once students’ orientations (e.g., academic, career, service) are profiled via HEO, institutions can align learning outcomes, pathways, and co-curricular options to each orientation</cite>. Use: create “intentional pathways” that flexibly route students to majors, minors, research, internships, or entrepreneurship tracks.

4.2 Self-realization and programming alignment
- Sphere prioritization: <cite id="547ab7bc-2">After computing average scores per sphere, universities can rank gaps (e.g., low learning or wellness realization) and reallocate resources (advising, tutoring, recreation, research opportunities) to elevate intentional pursuits</cite>. Use: annual student “realization audits” to recalibrate offerings.

4.3 Academic skills and SDL diagnostics
- Diagnostic questionnaires: <cite id="d225964d-1">Validated academic skills and SDL instruments allow targeted workshops (e.g., referencing, literature review, project management) and coaching for students with low SDL/efficacy</cite>. Use: integrate into first-year experiences and return-on-investment reviews.

4.4 Institutional climate and support
- Service quality and support: <cite id="d225964d-4">High-CVI/alpha questionnaires enable targeted improvement of academic preparedness, access, and support systems that foster intentional behavior</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Institutional questionnaires combining academic preparedness and support with student outcomes show excellent reliability and strong model fit, supporting continuous quality improvement</cite>. Use: dashboards linking support scores to retention/persistence.

5) Practical implementation: from survey to action

- Measurement cadence and cohorts: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Likert 1–5 Likert items for resolve, self-efficacy, belonging, and functioning can be fielded each semester as early-alert screens (e.g., Day 1 orientation, mid-semester, finals), enabling timely coaching and resource allocation</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-2">10-point self-realization questionnaires are student-friendly and can be embedded in LMS reflections to create longitudinal profiles</cite>.
- Predictive analytics: <cite id="547ab7bc-3">Combine AMS motivation subscales and personal resolve with UTAUT/TPB intention-to-use to model risk of disengagement or nonproductive tool adoption; validate with logistic regression/classifiers and iterate</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Track perceived goal attainment across academic/skill/social domains to quantify realized intentionality and link to GPA or course satisfaction via correlational analyses</cite>.
- Designing intentionally aligned experiences: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Use HEO profiles to align learning outcomes, co-curricular, and career services</cite>; <cite id="547ab7bc-2">use sphere ratings to prioritize space, staffing, and programming</cite>; <cite id="d225964d-1">use SDL/skills diagnostics to scaffold metacognitive strategies and skill-specific supports</cite>.
- Coaching and advising: <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Adapt “I have a strong desire to succeed” and “I will do whatever it takes” prompts into coaching goals, paired with self-efficacy and belonging interventions</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-4">When goal attainment falls short, investigate misalignment (learning vs. social expectations) and adjust pathways or support</cite>.

6) Building and validating your own “Intentional University” instruments

6.1 Instrument design patterns
- Start with purpose/orientation: <cite id="547ab7bc-0">Adapt HEO items to your institutional context via small-sample EFA/CAF to preserve factor structure and internal consistency</cite>.
- Add agency/motivation: <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">Adopt AMS-28 subscales (intrinsic, extrinsic, amotivation) and translate as needed, preserving 5-point Likert response format</cite>. <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Incorporate self-efficacy and resolve items validated in higher-education contexts</cite>.
- Close the loop with goals/satisfaction: <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Adopt goal attainment items across academic learning, skills, social life and validate via CFA/AVE/CR checks</cite>.
- Ensure fit and clarity: <cite id="d225964d-4">Conduct qualitative review (clarity, response options, coverage), then quantify content validity via I-CVI and S-CVI/Ave thresholds and refine</cite>. <cite id="d225964d-0">Pilot for internal consistency (alpha>.7), test CFA fit (e.g., GFI>.90, RMSEA<.10), convergent/discriminant validity, and iterate</cite>.

6.2 Validation and scaling checklist
- Content and face validity: <cite id="d225964d-4">Expert panels review relevance, clarity, and layout; achieve I-CVI≥.78 and S-CVI/Ave≥.90 as a benchmark</cite>.
- Reliability: <cite id="d225964d-0">Report Cronbach’s alpha per scale and overall; target alpha≥.70 per subscale and ≥.80 overall</cite>.
- Construct validity: <cite id="d225964d-0">Use CFA/EFA to confirm factor structure, AVE>0.5, CR>0.7, discriminant vs. convergent relationships</cite>.
- Invariance and generalizability: <cite id="3e85cbbd-3">Test measurement invariance across departments, years, and demographics to ensure fair comparisons</cite>.
- Pilot and iterate: <cite id="d225964d-0">Iterate item retention based on loadings, CR, AVE, and classification agreement to improve internal consistency and clarity</cite>.

7) Example toolkits and starter question banks

- Purpose and orientations:
  - HEO items (5 per orientation) and open-ended prompts to elicit values behind each orientation. <cite id="547ab7bc-0">The 25-item HEO offers five items per orientation and demonstrated internal consistency and practical deployment via an online platform</cite>.
- Agency and motivation:
  - Personal resolve: “I will do whatever it takes to master my academic studies at university.” “I have a strong desire to succeed in my academic studies at university.” <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Alpha≈.85 with 5-point Likert</cite>.
  - Self-efficacy: “I believe I will receive excellent grades in classes at this university.” <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Alpha≈.72</cite>.
  - Intrinsic/extrinsic motivation: AMS-28 item stems for “to know,” “accomplishment,” “stimulation,” “external,” “identified,” “introjected,” and “amotivation.” <cite id="3e85cbbd-1">AMS-28 established structure and reliability</cite>.
- Belonging and relating:
  - “I find it easy to relate to others at university.” <cite id="547ab7bc-1">Alpha≈.72</cite>.
- Goal attainment and satisfaction:
  - “My university meets my expectations for academic learning/skill development/social life.” <cite id="547ab7bc-4">Strong CR/AVE/alpha and factor loadings support use</cite>.
- Self-realization and programming fit:
  - Nine spheres (learning, sports-wellness, research, volunteer, etc.) rated 1–10; compute per-sphere averages and rank gaps. <cite id="547ab7bc-2">Validated with sample of 235 students</cite>.
- Intention to use and adoption:
  - UTAUT/TPB + behavioral intention items; combine with AMS motivation to model intention-to-engage. <cite id="547ab7bc-3">Content validity procedures and Likert scaling</cite>.

Title: Construction and Initial Validation of the Higher Education Orientations Questionnaire
Snippet: Orientations Questionnaire 

The goal of this study was to develop and initially test the HEO questionnaire. First, based on definitions of the five proposed higher education orientations and their corresponding predecessors, we prepared 10 or 11 statements in Hebrew per orientation, resulting in a 52-item version of the HEO questionnaire. Following Worthington and Whittaker (2006), after providing a brief definition for each dimension, we asked nine graduate students in career counseling and psychology to classify each of the 52 items into one of the five orientations to ensure the face and content validity of the items. This process revealed nine items that achieved an inter-judge agreement of less than 75%, resulting in their elimination. Next, the 43-item version of the HEO questionnaire was uploaded to the Future Directions website (www.kivunim.com), an anonymous and free self-help public service in Israel that aims at facilitating making better career decisions. 

After analyzing the questionnaire's psychometric properties, including an initial exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on a sample of 120 deliberating young adults, we removed 13 additional items because they decreased the internal consistency reliability of their supposed scale or loaded poorly on their factor. We repeated this process with another group of 182 deliberating individuals, removing and revising items to enhance the scales' internal consistency reliability and factor loadings, resulting in a 25-item version of the questionnaire, with five items per scale. In the following sections, we report the findings derived from this 25-item version, based on the responses of an additional large sample of deliberating young adults. The research was approved by the IRB of the Hebrew University (#82015G2).

Evaluating the proposed answers, students thereby evaluate each of the possible spheres for selfrealization at the University. The results processing consists in calculating the average values of points for each of the 9 spheres of intra-University activity. As a result, a rating of these spheres is compiled in terms of their subjective significance for the self-realization of students at the University. This authors' method was developed as a questionnaire, which is aimed at identifying the students' subjective attitude to University education in terms of the possibilities of revealing and realizing their internal potential, as well as developing themselves as successful and competent subjects (Shutenko A. and Shutenko E., 2008). Title: Examining Students’ Acceptance and Use of ChatGPT in Saudi Arabian Higher Education
Snippet: The survey adopted in this research has three sections. The first section outlines the research objectives and guidelines needed for completing the survey. Throughout the second section, information about participants' profile is gathered. The third section of the study involved investigating various aspects, with a rating of 1 representing "strongly disagree" and a rating of 5 indicating "strongly agree". The ChatGPT UTAUT scale was adopted from Venkatesh et al. [13] and includes four variables: PE, EE, SI, and FC. In addition to these variables, the ChatGPT TPB scale also includes a behavioral intention variable adopted from Ajzen and Fishbein [36] as well as an intent-to-use variable developed from previous studies [22]. To verify the consistency and ease of use of the survey, the survey was subjected to evaluation by professors and education leaders. In order to maintain the validity of the survey's content, certain statements' wording was modified and arranged based upon the responses of participants and scholars [37].

Title: How perceived goal attainment shapes student satisfaction: the chain mediating roles of competence acquisition, learning, and infrastructure
Snippet: The measurement of students' perceived goal attainment was initially developed through expert focus group discussions and a comprehensive review of relevant literature. The preliminary version of the scale consisted of five items covering students' expectations for various aspects of HEIs life. An initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) indicated that the measurement model required improvement, with fit indices showing GFI = 0.959, AGFI = 0.878, and RMSEA = 0.139. In line with established recommendations, items with low factor loadings or conceptual overlap were removed. Specifically, two items-"My university meets my expectations for campus life" and "I can achieve my established goals at my university"-were deleted based on factor loadings and expert consensus. 

The final version of the scale retained 3 items: "My university meets my expectations for academic learning," "My university meets my expectations for skill development, " and "My university meets my expectations for social life." Each item was rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from "1 = strongly disagree" to "5 = strongly agree, " with higher scores indicating greater levels of perceived goal attainment. Due to the small number of indicators, the CFA model degrees of freedom were limited; therefore, the construct validity was primarily evaluated using standardized factor loadings, composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE). The standardized factor loadings were 0.92, 0.96, and 0.92, respectively, with corresponding squared multiple correlations (R 2 ) of 0.851, 0.919, and 0.838. The computed CR was 0.95 (>0.70) (Hair et al., 2018) and the AVE was 0.87 (>0.50) (Fornell and Larcker, 1981), demonstrating satisfactory convergent validity. Moreover, the scale exhibited excellent internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.95.

Title: Does socioeconomic status influence students’ access to residential college and ameliorate performance discrepancies among them in China?
Snippet: The questionnaire used in this study was derived from validated scales employed in a previous study [38,52]. It includes three parts associated with the study framework. In the initial part, respondents provide personal information, covering aspects such as gender, ethnicity, family district, and academic performance. Academic achievement is assessed based on Cumulative Grade-Point Average (CGPA) with a 4-point scale, following existing literature on education economics [1]. To guarantee data accuracy, this part includes respondents' names and student ID, facilitating the retrieval of accurate CGPA data from academic records at the sampled institutions. The second part refers to SES, encompassing parental monthly income, education attainments, and occupation, across five dimensions. The final part assesses the RCs forming part of the living environment, faculty interaction, peer interaction, and co-curricular activities, across four dimensions. Title: Construction and Standardization a Students' Academic Skills Assessment Scale for a University of Medical Sciences
Snippet: Its psychometric properties (retest validity 0.98, Cronbach's alpha, 0.98) were validated and its factorial validity was confirmed. 

Behar-Horenstein, Beck and Su [40] conducted an initial validation of the Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning for Pharmacy Education. Hence, the revised 55-item SRSSDL was a valid and homogenous scale of pharmacy students' self-directed learning within one pharmacy program.

2-How valid is the questionnaire made on this basis? 

3-To what degree does the questionnaire on academic skills have internal consistency? 

4-What kind of factor structure does the questionnaire have?

Title: Psychometric Properties of an Instrument for Assessing University Administrators’ Knowledge on Gender-Based Violence
Snippet: This study aimed to conduct a psychometric validation of the 'Questionnaire for the Evaluation of Institutional Agents' Knowledge about Violence in the University' (QUEST VBG UNIV). This instrument, constructed based on a literature review and a qualitative phase of the research, originally had a structure comprising four dimensions. However, these were not confirmed by the Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), with parallel analysis indicating two factors. Despite the ambiguous results regarding the adequacy of EFA for the sample data (with favorable results in Bartlett's test and mediocre outcomes in Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure), all other evaluations demonstrated a high degree of stability and reproducibility of the two factors obtained. These assessments included tests of composite reliability, ORION, Factorial Discriminant Index (FDI), and Latent and Observed H, internal consistency (using the omega coefficient), and a satisfactory or near-ideal model fit (as shown by RMSEA, Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and chi-square tests). Furthermore, the tests confirmed the non-unidimensional character of the questionnaire (UniCo, ECV, and MIREAL tests). 

From the 38 items in the original composition of QUEST VBG UNIV, 19 were retained in the final questionnaire's two factors (see Supplementary Material 2). Several potential elements may have led to the non-retention of items. One aspect is the similarity in the wording of some questions, although this was mitigated by the interview format of the questionnaire application, facilitated with interviewer guidance. 

Another aspect is the structuring of the questions, some of which had ordinal responses while others were qualitative in nature. This could have interfered with normality and variances among the items, as qualitative variables did not necessarily follow an ordinal configuration. To minimize this, we used a robust factorial analysis and the Robust Diagonally Weighted Least Squares (RDWLS) extraction method, which considers the ordinal nature of the variables and adjusts the data to a normal distribution (40)(41) . 

Sample size is another consideration.

Title: Institutional Determinants of Academic Achievement in Biomedical Sciences: A Cross-Sectional Study of Nursing Students in Uganda
Snippet: A structured questionnaire was used to collect data. The questionnaire was developed by the principal investigator based on the existing literature and validated by two co-authors and two peer researchers, all of whom were experts in nursing education. This single questionnaire was used to collect data across the three biomedical science courses. The questionnaire consisted four sections, labeled A, B, C, and D. Section A gathered data on the students' sociodemographic characteristics and consisted 20 items. Section B assessed the level of academic achievement, comprising 4 broad items, each with at least four sub items. Section C focused on the student-related educational factors that predicted academic achievement and contained 28 items. Data from this section formed the basis for the previously published article. Section D examined institutional determinants of academic achievement and included 29 items. Data from this section form the basis for this article. 

The questionnaire was pre-tested with 30 nursing students from a non-participating university to ensure its clarity and reliability. The scale's internal consistency was assessed, yielding a Cronbach's alpha value of 0.9366, indicating excellent reliability. A structured questionnaire was used to ensure standardized and reliable data collection, minimize bias, and enhancing consistency. 52 Its high Cronbach's alpha (≥ 0.80) reflected strong internal consistency, indicating that the instrument reliably measured key constructs such as institutional support and academic preparedness. 53 This reliability reduced measurement errors, strengthened internal and construct validity, and ensured that the findings were both accurate and meaningful. 54 By using a psychometrically sound instrument, the study improved methodological rigor and credibility, enabling trustworthy conclusions that can inform nursing education policies and practice. 55

Title: Service Quality and Students’ Satisfaction in Private Lebanese Higher Education Institutions: The Case of X University
Snippet: The draft questionnaire was checked for content validity by five jurors. Three of them were instructors with Ph.Ds (two education instructors and one business instructor) at two private Lebanese universities, and the rest were Ph.D. holders and candidate in education at the Lebanese University. Content validation of the draft questionnaire consisted of two consecutive phases: qualitative then quantitative. 

The qualitative phase comprised the following areas: appropriateness of directions for the questionnaire, appropriateness and completeness of content areas, appropriateness and clarity of questionnaire items, adequacy of response options, opportunity for revision, deletion, and addition of items, and opportunity for additional comments. The qualitative review resulted in revision of 15 items in all dimensions except program issues, breaking one item in reputation dimension into two distinct items, deletion of two items from the dimensions of non-academic aspects and student satisfaction, and addition of one item to the dimension of access. 

The quantitative review required jurors to rate the relevance of items of the revised questionnaire to the measured dimensions using a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 for 'not relevant' to 4 for 'highly relevant'. The relevance score of 1 or 2 was recorded as 0, and the relevance of score of 3 or 4 was recorded as 1 (Yusoff, 2019). Content validity index (CVI) was then calculated for each item (I-CVI) and scale (S-CVI/Ave). According to Polit et al. (2007), a scale should have I-CVIs of .78 or higher and an S-CVI/Ave of .90 or higher for three or more experts to be considered of good content validity. All items got an I-CVI ranging from .80 to 1 and an S-CVI/Ave of .95. Hence, the revised questionnaire had high content validity. 

The revised questionnaire was also checked for face validity by six X University SoED students. Face validation were conducted based on the following criteria: reasonableness and clarity of items, adequacy of instructions, accuracy of language, and appropriateness of layout (Oluwatayo, 2012). Consequently, the revised questionnaire was found to be having high face validity.

Title: Adaptation and validation of the academic motivation scale for higher education across four Eastern European countries
Snippet: No content available

Title: Perceived academic support and academic achievement among Ethiopian first-year university students: the serial mediating roles of academic motivation and resilience
Snippet: The Multidimensional Academic Motivation Scale (AMS-28;Vallerand et al., 1992) was adapted and validated by Orsini (2016) for university settings. This study further adapted it locally to assess students' reasons for pursuing education. The 28-item scale, scored on a 5-point scale (1 = not at all corresponds, 5 = corresponds exactly), includes intrinsic motivation (12 items: to know, accomplishment, stimulation), extrinsic motivation (12 items: external, identified, introjected regulation), and amotivation (4 items). Higher scores indicate stronger motivation types. Reliability and validity were established previously (Vallerand et al., 1992;Orsini, 2016) and confirmed here.

Title: Emotion regulation and perceptions of academic stress as key predictors of academic motivation in second language learning
Snippet: To reduce semantic redundancy, two items were removed from the original 18-item Perception of Academic Stress Scale. Specifically, item 7 ("Teachers have unrealistic expectations of me") was excluded due to its overlap with item 6, which also reflects pressure from teachers. Similarly, item 11 ("I believe that the amount of work assignments is too much") was removed because of its conceptual similarity to item 10, which addresses excessive curriculum workload more broadly. The final version of the scale thus contains 16 items. In our sample, the scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.962). A confirmatory factor analysis was conducted and demonstrated an acceptable fit (χ²/df = 2.04, RMSEA = 0.045, SRMR = 0.031, CFI = 0.964, and TLI = 0.956). 

The Academic Motivation Scale, created by Vallerand et al. in 1992, is a well-established tool used to evaluate academic motivation [35]. It includes 28 items that measure motivation in three core areas: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and amotivation. From the original 28-item Academic Motivation Scale, three items were removed to reduce redundancy. Item 6 ("For the pleasure I experience while surpassing myself in learning English") was conceptually similar to item 13, which more clearly emphasizes personal accomplishment. Item 20 ("To show myself that I am an intelligent person capable of mastering English") overlapped with other items focused on self-validation, such as item 7. Item 21 ("In order to have a better salary that English skills can help me achieve") duplicated content found in items addressing career-related external goals (e.g., item 1 and item 8). These deletions resulted in a refined 25-item scale. Although the Academic Motivation Scale is based on a multidimensional model of motivation, we used a composite score of academic motivation in the current study. This approach was supported by prior research suggesting that, in some educational contexts, the subscales of the Academic Motivation Scale may form a second-order general motivation factor [36,37].

Title: Adaptation and validation of the academic motivation scale for higher education across four Eastern European countries
Snippet: The article focuses on adaptation and validation of the Academic Motivation Scale questionnaire (AMS‐28) in higher education in four Eastern European countries: Czechia, Slovakia, Serbia, and Poland. The research was conducted with a total of 1711 respondents. We examined the construct validity of AMS‐28 including measurement invariance and reliability according to national, gender and age groups. Our analysis confirmed its original seven‐factor structure as well as its reliability. The tool is measurement invariant across all compared groups (gender, age, countries) except Poland, whose results are specific. The results identify new places on the world map where AMS‐28 is functional. The tool appears functional in time, space and various language mutations. snippet.text:
To reduce semantic redundancy, two items were removed from the original 18-item Perception of Academic Stress Scale. Specifically, item 7 ("Teachers have unrealistic expectations of me") was excluded due to its overlap with item 6, which also reflects pressure from teachers. Similarly, item 11 ("I believe that the amount of work assignments is too much") was removed because of its conceptual similarity to item 10, which addresses excessive curriculum workload more broadly. The final version of the scale thus contains 16 items. In our sample, the scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.962). A confirmatory factor analysis was conducted and demonstrated an acceptable fit (χ²/df = 2.04, RMSEA = 0.045, SRMR = 0.031, CFI = 0.964, and TLI = 0.956). 

The Academic Motivation Scale, created by Vallerand et al. in 1992, is a well-established tool used to evaluate academic motivation [35]. It includes 28 items that measure motivation in three core areas: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and amotivation. From the original 28-item Academic Motivation Scale, three items were removed to reduce redundancy. Item 6 ("For the pleasure I experience while surpassing myself in learning English") was conceptually similar to item 13, which more clearly emphasizes personal accomplishment. Item 20 ("To show myself that I am an intelligent person capable of mastering English") overlapped with other items focused on self-validation, such as item 7. Item 21 ("In order to have a better salary that English skills can help me achieve") duplicated content found in items addressing career-related external goals (e.g., item 1 and item 8). These deletions resulted in a refined 25-item scale. Although the Academic Motivation Scale is based on a multidimensional model of motivation, we used a composite score of academic motivation in the current study. This approach was supported by prior research suggesting that, in some educational contexts, the subscales of the Academic Motivation Scale may form a second-order general motivation factor [36,37].
