attempts.answer:
Summary and bottom line
Intentionality in undergraduate learning is most often operationalized through four validated families of measures: (a) instruments grounded in Intentional Learning Theory (e.g., the Learning Orientation Questionnaire, LOQ), which target a unitary trait of intentional learning; (b) agency-for-learning scales that separate planfulness from decision confidence; (c) self-regulated learning batteries (e.g., MSLQ and related SRL instruments) that capture intentionality via goal-directed strategy selection, organization, and monitoring; and (d) persistence/intention-to-continue measures that index future-directed academic continuation rather than effortful learning per se. These families often yield conflicting item-level patterns because they weigh different facets of intentionality (process vs outcome orientation, trait vs state, effortful control vs evaluative persistence), use distinct psychometric models, and embed constructs within different theoretical frameworks. <cite id="8f33e454-0">LOQ was developed by subject-matter experts and psychometricians and shows high validity and reliability for measuring “Intentional Learning” as a unitary construct</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-2">LOQ determines where learners fall along a learning orientation continuum, with evidence of reliability and validity under best-practice criteria</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-3">Validation is an ongoing process as theoretical abstractions (intentional learning) evolve with neuroscience; LOQ evidence substantiates use as a valid measure of a position along transforming, performing, conforming, or resistant learners</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-4">An agency-for-learning intentionality scale among post-secondary students bifurcates into Planfulness and Decision Confidence subscales, each reliable and modestly correlated</cite> <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ evidence across undergraduate and clinical populations shows acceptable fit and reliability, with validation noted as context-specific</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-1">ASPECT identifies “personal effort” as one of three factors, illustrating how engagement instruments can capture intentionality-related effort facets</cite> <cite id="7752ae541-1">Undergraduate persistence is often proxied by intention-to-continue items (e.g., willingness to repeat studies) with acceptable reliability</cite>.

Candidate validated scales and what they measure
Intentional Learning Theory (LOQ). LOQ is explicitly designed to measure “Intentional Learning” as a theoretical construct, with content assembled and reviewed by experts and validated via multiple sources of evidence: content validity, item performance, dimensionality (e.g., PCA), internal consistency, and criterion-related consistency with related constructs. It treats intentionality as a unitary trait-like orientation that supports higher-order thinking and lifelong learning, positioning learners along a continuum (transforming, performing, conforming, resistant). This yields a compact latent variable reflecting the learner’s propensity to engage in directed, effortful learning and to shift strategies purposefully. <cite id="8f33e454-0">LOQ’s psychometric analyses accumulate sources of validity evidence and demonstrate high validity for measuring Intentional Learning</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-2">LOQ provides reliability and validity evidence consistent with best practices and interprets scores along a learning orientation continuum</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-3">LOQ validity rests on a theoretical framework whose constructs can evolve; nonetheless, findings substantiate use as a valid measure of position along the continuum</cite>.

Agency-for-learning (planfulness and decision confidence). In post-secondary samples, selected intention-related items from classic instruments load into two distinct factors: Planfulness (e.g., setting goals, organizing tasks) and Decision Confidence (e.g., self-efficacy about choices), each with strong internal consistency and a small positive correlation. This operationalization emphasizes momentary decision-making with perceived control and readiness, making “intentionality” a composite of strategic structuring and motivational self-efficacy rather than a unitary trait. <cite id="8f33e454-4">An EFA on post-secondary students revealed a two-factor intentionality structure: Planfulness (α = 0.82) and Decision Confidence (α = 0.82), with r = 0.357, p < 0.01 between factors</cite>.

Self-regulated learning instruments (MSLQ and variants). Widely used SRL batteries explicitly capture intentionality through cognitive and metacognitive strategies (e.g., organizing, elaboration, monitoring), goal-directed effort regulation, and managerial behaviors. LOQ’s developers highlight that validation is context-specific; similar findings appear in MSLQ validation among medical undergraduates and clinical learners, where reliability and fit are acceptable but may require local adaptation. These instruments make intentionality operational through item-level tactics (e.g., “use outlines,” “self-testing”), which can be validated in new contexts but retain their process emphasis. <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ’s motivation and strategy scales show acceptable goodness-of-fit and reliability, with validation emphasized as context-specific across undergraduate, clinical, and postgraduate learners</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-1">ASPECT’s “personal effort” factor (with value and instructor contribution) shows how engagement measures capture effort-directed facets often labeled intentionality</cite>.

Persistence and continuation measures. “Intention to persist” captures an outcome-oriented form of intentionality—students’ expectation to continue or repeat a program despite difficulties. These items (e.g., satisfaction with choice; willingness to repeat studies) demonstrate acceptable reliability and function as a proximal indicator of retention, highlighting that intentionality can be framed as future-directed continuation rather than as the process quality of studying. <cite id="23e179a8-2">Intention to persist was measured by Neuville’s eight-item scale (e.g., “Even if I didn’t pass this year, I would start the same studies all over again”), with alpha = 0.85 and 1–7 response scale</cite> <cite id="23e179a8-0">Psychometric validation procedures (CFA, reliability, criterion validity via associations with intention to leave STEM) were used to support persistence-related measures</cite>.

Why operationalizations conflict: constructs, levels, and methods
Intentionality as trait vs. process and outcome. LOQ treats intentionality as a stable orientation; agency-for-learning splits it into planfulness (structural) and decision confidence (motivational efficacy); SRL instruments capture tactic-level goal-directed regulation; persistence scales index continuation intentions. These different scopes produce divergent loadings and factor structures, even when labeled “intentionality.” <cite id="8f33e454-2">LOQ operationalizes intentionality as a position along a learning orientation continuum</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-4">Post-secondary intentionality factors into planfulness and decision confidence</cite> <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ’s strategy and motivation subscales emphasize tactic-level regulation with context-specific validity</cite> <cite id="23e179a8-2">Persistence items reflect proximal intention to continue studies despite difficulties</cite>.

Effortful, strategy-based control vs. evaluative persistence. “Intentionality” can mean “deliberate, effortful regulation of study” (LOQ, MSLQ) or “resolve to continue despite challenges” (persistence scales). Under stress or failure, people may intend to persist at continuing (high persistence) yet show low planfulness or strategic effort (low intentionality in process terms), producing conflicting patterns across instruments. <cite id="23e179a8-2">Intention to persist is proximal to actual persistence and assessed via continuation-oriented statements</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-4">Planfulness and decision confidence capture distinct facets of intentionality with a modest correlation</cite>.

Intentional vs. incidental learning distinction vs. everyday academic tasks. Intentional learning theory differentiates learning that is purpose-driven (intentional) from learning that occurs incidentally; however, classroom learning often blends both, and items tapping “purpose/purposeful practice” can map differently across cohorts and contexts. Title: Boy–Girl Differences in Pictorial Verbal Learning in Students Aged 8–12 Years and the Influence of Parental Education
Snippet: Intentional learning is of key importance for the acquisition of new information and for academic performance. The process of intentional learning can typically be described as having the purpose of learning information and committing it to one's memory (Thomas and Rohwer, 1986;Lezak et al., 2012;Hampshire et al., 2016). This is different from incidental learning, which is the accidental learning of information while actually concentrating on other information (Thomas and Rohwer, 1986;Lezak et al., 2012;Hampshire et al., 2016;Ahmed, 2017;Kontaxopoulou et al., 2017). The ability of intentional learning typically improves with experience and with age (Meijer et al., 2006(Meijer et al., , 2007;;Meijs et al., 2013Meijs et al., , 2016;;Blachstein and Vakil, 2016). It appears that there are major individual differences in the pace at which intentional learning develops at the end of childhood and the beginning of adolescence (Meijer et al., 2007;Jolles, 2016;Meijs et al., 2016;Juraska and Willing, 2017). 

Individual differences in intentional learning performance may contribute to individual variations in the ability to acquire and consolidate new information at school, as well as in learning motivation and school achievement. Examples of intentional learning at school is when students have to learn lists of words that belong to a new language and when they have to learn lists of conjugations of verbs. Another example of intentional learning at school is when new mathematical rules and multiplication tables need to be learned. Students with poor intentional learning ability may experience profound difficulties with learning lists of new words, conjugations of verbs as well as with learning new mathematical rules and lists of tables. This may negatively affect their language and mathematic performance as well as their learning motivation (Lawrence et al., 2015). It is therefore of importance to find out whether students are characterized by individual differences in intentional learning performance, and whether there are external factors that contribute to these individual differences. Identification of external factors could allow early detection of those individuals who are at risk of poor intentional learning performance, and thus also for problems with learning at school.

Title: Psychometric Properties of the Science Self-Efficacy Scale for STEMM Undergraduates
Snippet: Studies have found that science self-efficacy corresponds with a higher likelihood of pursuing a researchfocused career for both undergraduate and graduate/doctoral students (Adedokun et al., 2013;Chemers et al., 2011;Estrada et al., 2011). Additionally, studies have examined the relationship between science self-efficacy and other psychosocial measures such as science identity (Chemers, 2006) to obtain a more complete understanding of students' scientific training trajectories (Estrada et al., 2011). 

Validation studies that conduct a thorough examination of the psychometric properties of a scale are important because they ensure that the scale measures the target concept and appropriately represents the characteristics of its intended audience (AERA et al., 2014). Clarity on whether the scale used in a study has well-established psychometric properties and whether the scale operates similarly in different subgroups of a population ultimately enhances the trustworthiness of the results and implications of studies that employ validated scales. 

The current study examines the psychometric properties of the Science Self-Efficacy Scale (SSES), initially developed by Chemers et al. (2011) with 10 items and adapted into a six-item scale by Estrada et al. (2011). This six-item scale was used in the Enhance Diversity Study (EDS), a program assessment examining biomedical research capacity-building initiatives at 11 higher education institutions across the United States. At the time of the EDS, the adapted six-item SSES had not yet been validated using a large, national sample of diverse undergraduate students. 

We conducted a comprehensive validation of the scale by examining (a) construct validity, which includes an analysis of reliability coefficients, fitting an item response theory model, and assessing measurement invariance of how the scale functions across various subgroups, such as gender and race/ethnicity; (b) dimensionality using a cross-validation approach; and (c) validity based on other related traits or outcomes. By employing an item response theory framework, we were able to examine the specific item characteristics of the SSES and its relationship to the science self-efficacy latent construct. The results of this validation study provide critical information for researchers, evaluators, faculty, and administrators involved in initiatives that aim to facilitate retention in scientific career training environments.

Title: Bored to Be Wild: How Boredom Is Related to Pre-Service Teachers’ Intention to Persist in Their Studies
Snippet: All analyses were performed on R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using the lavaan package [45]. We performed a mediation analysis with structural equation modeling (SEM) to test (1) how control and value predicted boredom, and (2) how boredom was related to the intention to persist at university. We hypothesized that (1) the more participants felt a lack of control and low in value, the higher their boredom and (2) the more intense their boredom, the lower their intention to persist. We further hypothesized that both control and value would be positively related to the intention to persist (see Figure 1). 

Intention to persist in the university was measured using the scale used by Neuville [23,44]. Intention to persist can be considered as a proximal measure of actual persistence [23]. This scale consists of eight items such as: "Even if I didn't pass this year, I would start the same studies all over again", and "With two months of hindsight, I am satisfied with my choice". Four items were reversed, such as, "If I had known at the beginning of the year what I know now, I would have made another study choice". The scale presented acceptable reliability (alpha = 0.85). Participants were asked to answer on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
</snippet>

Title: The Influence of Microaffirmations on Undergraduate Persistence in Science Career Pathways
Snippet: The present studies aimed to advance the measurement and understanding of microaffirmation kindness cues and assessed how they related to historically underrepresented (HU) and historically overrepresented (HO) undergraduate student persistence in science-related career pathways. Study 1 developed and tested the dimensionality of a new Microaffirmations Scale. Study 2 confirmed the two-factor structure of the Microaffirmations Scale and demonstrated that the scale possessed measurement invariance across HU and HO students. Further, the scale was administered as part of a longitudinal design spanning 9 months, with results showing that students’ reported microaffirmations did not directly predict higher intentions to persist in science-related career pathways 9 months later. However, scientific self-efficacy and identity, measures of student integration into the science community, mediated this relationship. Overall, our results demonstrated that microaffirmations can be measured in an academic context and that these experiences have predictive value when they increase students’ integration into their science communities, ultimately resulting in greater intentions to persist 9 months later. Researchers and practitioners can use the Microaffirmations Scale for future investigations to increase understanding of the positive contextual factors that can ultimately help reduce persistence gaps in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics degree attainment.
</snippet></tool_output>

Sufficiency check: I have gathered evidence on four operational families of “intentionality” measures used with undergraduates: (1) LOQ (intentional learning theory), (2) agency-for-learning intentionality (planfulness + decision confidence), (3) self-regulated learning batteries (MSLQ, SRL-IS) that capture intention via goal-directed strategies/organization/monitoring, and (4) adjacent persistence/intention-to-continue measures that operationalize “intentionality” as future-directed academic continuation rather than effortful learning per se. I also have evidence that engagement instruments sometimes include “personal effort” facets and that reflection/insight measures can drift constructively, explaining cross-scale conflicts. I will synthesize these with explicit contrasts and mechanisms of conflict (construct scope, level of abstraction, and methodological choices). Structure: 
- Overview and bottom-line
- Candidate validated scales and what they measure
- Why operationalizations conflict (construct scope, process/outcome emphasis, methodological artifacts, context-specificity)
- Choosing and aligning measures in undergraduate research
Each evidence-bearing claim will be cited to retrieved snippets.

Summary and bottom line
Intentionality in undergraduate learning is most often operationalized through four validated families of measures: (a) instruments grounded in Intentional Learning Theory (e.g., the Learning Orientation Questionnaire, LOQ), which target a unitary trait of intentional learning; (b) agency-for-learning scales that separate planfulness from decision confidence; (c) self-regulated learning batteries (e.g., MSLQ and related SRL instruments) that capture intentionality via goal-directed strategy selection, organization, and monitoring; and (d) persistence/intention-to-continue measures that index future-directed academic continuation rather than effortful learning per se. These families often yield conflicting item-level patterns because they weigh different facets of intentionality (process vs outcome orientation, trait vs state, effortful control vs evaluative persistence), use distinct psychometric models, and embed constructs within different theoretical frameworks. <cite id="8f33e454-0">LOQ was developed by subject-matter experts and psychometricians and shows high validity and reliability for measuring “Intentional Learning” as a unitary construct</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-2">LOQ determines where learners fall along a learning orientation continuum, with evidence of reliability and validity under best-practice criteria</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-3">Validation is an ongoing process as theoretical abstractions (intentional learning) evolve with neuroscience; LOQ evidence substantiates use as a valid measure of a position along transforming, performing, conforming, or resistant learners</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-4">An agency-for-learning intentionality scale among post-secondary students bifurcates into Planfulness and Decision Confidence subscales, each reliable and modestly correlated</cite> <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ evidence across undergraduate and clinical populations shows acceptable fit and reliability, with validation noted as context-specific</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-1">ASPECT identifies “personal effort” as one of three factors, illustrating how engagement instruments can capture intentionality-related effort facets</cite> <cite id="7752ae541-1">Undergraduate persistence is often proxied by intention-to-continue items (e.g., willingness to repeat studies) with acceptable reliability</cite>.

Candidate validated scales and what they measure
Intentional Learning Theory (LOQ). LOQ is explicitly designed to measure “Intentional Learning” as a theoretical construct, with content assembled and reviewed by experts and validated via multiple sources of evidence: content validity, item performance, dimensionality (e.g., PCA), internal consistency, and criterion-related consistency with related constructs. It treats intentionality as a unitary trait-like orientation that supports higher-order thinking and lifelong learning, positioning learners along a continuum (transforming, performing, conforming, resistant). This yields a compact latent variable reflecting the learner’s propensity to engage in directed, effortful learning and to shift strategies purposefully. <cite id="8f33e454-0">LOQ’s psychometric analyses accumulate sources of validity evidence and demonstrate high validity for measuring Intentional Learning</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-2">LOQ provides reliability and validity evidence consistent with best practices and interprets scores along a learning orientation continuum</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-3">LOQ validity rests on a theoretical framework whose constructs can evolve; nonetheless, findings substantiate use as a valid measure of position along the continuum</cite>.

Agency-for-learning (planfulness and decision confidence). In post-secondary samples, selected intention-related items from classic instruments load into two distinct factors: Planfulness (e.g., setting goals, organizing tasks) and Decision Confidence (e.g., self-efficacy about choices), each with strong internal consistency and a small positive correlation. This operationalization emphasizes momentary decision-making with perceived control and readiness, making “intentionality” a composite of strategic structuring and motivational self-efficacy rather than a unitary trait. <cite id="8f33e454-4">An EFA on post-secondary students revealed a two-factor intentionality structure: Planfulness (α = 0.82) and Decision Confidence (α = 0.82), with r = 0.357, p < 0.01 between factors</cite>.

Self-regulated learning instruments (MSLQ and variants). Widely used SRL batteries explicitly capture intentionality through cognitive and metacognitive strategies (e.g., organizing, elaboration, monitoring), goal-directed effort regulation, and managerial behaviors. LOQ’s developers highlight that validation is context-specific; similar findings appear in MSLQ validation among medical undergraduates and clinical learners, where reliability and fit are acceptable but may require local adaptation. These instruments make intentionality operational through item-level tactics (e.g., “use outlines,” “self-testing”), which can be validated in new contexts but retain their process emphasis. <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ’s motivation and strategy scales show acceptable goodness-of-fit and reliability, with validation emphasized as context-specific across undergraduate, clinical, and postgraduate learners</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-1">ASPECT’s “personal effort” factor (with value and instructor contribution) shows how engagement measures capture effort-directed facets often labeled intentionality</cite>.

Persistence and continuation measures. “Intention to persist” captures an outcome-oriented form of intentionality—students’ expectation to continue or repeat a program despite difficulties. These items (e.g., satisfaction with choice; willingness to repeat studies) demonstrate acceptable reliability and function as a proximal indicator of retention, highlighting that intentionality can be framed as future-directed continuation rather than as the process quality of studying. <cite id="23e179a8-2">Intention to persist was measured by Neuville’s eight-item scale (e.g., “Even if I didn’t pass this year, I would start the same studies all over again”), with alpha = 0.85 and 1–7 response scale</cite> <cite id="23e179a8-0">Psychometric validation procedures (CFA, reliability, criterion validity via associations with intention to leave STEM) were used to support persistence-related measures</cite>.

Why operationalizations conflict: constructs, levels, and methods
Intentionality as trait vs. process and outcome. LOQ treats intentionality as a stable orientation; agency-for-learning splits it into planfulness (structural) and decision confidence (motivational efficacy); SRL instruments capture tactic-level goal-directed regulation; persistence scales index continuation intentions. These different scopes produce divergent loadings and factor structures, even when labeled “intentionality.” <cite id="8f33e454-2">LOQ operationalizes intentionality as a position along a learning orientation continuum</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-4">Post-secondary intentionality factors into planfulness and decision confidence</cite> <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ’s strategy and motivation subscales emphasize tactic-level regulation with context-specific validity</cite> <cite id="23e179a8-2">Persistence items reflect proximal intention to continue studies despite difficulties</cite>.

Effortful, strategy-based control vs. evaluative persistence. “Intentionality” can mean “deliberate, effortful regulation of study” (LOQ, MSLQ) or “resolve to continue despite challenges” (persistence scales). Under stress or failure, people may intend to persist at continuing (high persistence) yet show low planfulness or strategic effort (low intentionality in process terms), producing conflicting patterns across instruments. <cite id="23e179a8-2">Intention to persist is proximal to actual persistence and assessed via continuation-oriented statements</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-4">Planfulness and decision confidence capture distinct facets of intentionality with a modest correlation</cite>.

Intentional vs. incidental learning distinction vs. everyday academic tasks. Intentional learning theory differentiates learning that is purpose-driven (intentional) from learning that occurs incidentally; however, classroom learning often blends both, and items tapping “purpose/purposeful practice” can map differently across cohorts and contexts. Cross-cultural adaptations (e.g., LOQ, engagement scales) show that local validity requires item refinement, altering factor structures and interpretations. <cite id="637ee541-1">Intentional learning is purposeful acquisition and committing to memory, distinct from incidental learning; ability improves with age and experience</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-0">LOQ’s content and validation were iteratively refined across groups</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-0">UWES-S and CSES show robust reliability and adaptation for undergraduates, but their constructs (engagement, core self-evaluations) are distinct from pure intentionality</cite>.

Methodological artifacts: model choice, rotation, and context-specificity. Different psychometric strategies (PCA vs CFA, oblique vs varimax rotation, single-factor vs two-factor) and theoretical commitments can yield different item clusters; agency-for-learning’s two-factor model arises under EFA with varimax and acceptable alpha, while LOQ supports a unitary factor under oblique rotation. LOQ authors emphasize that validity accrues as degrees across multiple sources; nonetheless, construct drift and evolving theory can make latent structures appear different across samples and time. <cite id="8f33e454-4">EFA with Varimax rotation on post-secondary students yielded planfulness and decision confidence subscales</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-1">ASPECT used oblique promax rotation to allow correlated engagement aspects, revealing value, personal effort, and instructor contribution</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-3">LOQ validity is argued cumulatively across multiple facets, and theoretical frameworks evolve, influencing construct interpretation</cite>.

Cross-instrument overlap and boundary-crossing constructs. Engagement instruments include “personal effort,” which overlaps with intentionality but also incorporates value and instructor contribution; reflection/insight instruments (e.g., SRIS) show that factor structures and factor labels can change across settings, underscoring that items labeled “intentional” may load on reflection or insight instead of effortful goal pursuit. <cite id="7752ae51-1">ASPECT’s EFA found personal effort, value of group activity, and instructor contribution as factors</cite> <cite id="7752ae51-3">SRIS validity and factor labels varied across contexts; interpretations of scores depend on validity arguments and setting</cite>.

Choosing and aligning measures
- If your goal is to capture a unitary trait-like orientation tied to purposeful, higher-order learning, use LOQ; it integrates across tactics and dispositions and is grounded in intentional learning theory. <cite id="8f33e454-0">LOQ provides content validity, item quality, dimensionality, and reliability evidence for Intentional Learning</cite> <cite id="8f33e454-2">Scores indicate position along a learning orientation continuum</cite>.
- If you need proximal, class-room applicable facets, use agency-for-learning’s planfulness and decision confidence to separate structural planning from motivational self-efficacy. <cite id="8f33e454-4">Planfulness and Decision Confidence each show high internal consistency and modest intercorrelation</cite>.
- If your construct is “goal-directed regulation” in coursework, adopt SRL batteries (e.g., MSLQ) and validate locally; they offer detailed, process-level items and show acceptable fit and reliability with undergraduate populations. <cite id="637ee541-4">MSLQ strategy and motivation scales show acceptable model fit and reliability, with context-specific validation emphasized</cite>.
- If your construct is “intention to continue,” use intention-to-persist measures; interpret them as proximal indicators of retention and analyze them via CFA/reliability and criterion validity (e.g., against intention to leave). <cite id="23e179a8-2">An eight-item intention-to-persist scale with alpha = 0.85 operationalizes proximal persistence</cite> <cite id="23e179a8-0">Validation via CFA, reliability, and criterion validity to intention to leave supports use</cite>.

Practical guidance: align to theory and outcome. Map your research question to a theoretical definition—trait-like intentional learning (LOQ), process control (MSLQ), decisional self-efficacy (agency), or continuation intention (persistence)—then select or assemble items that match that scope. Expect cross-scale conflicts when mixing trait and state, process and outcome, or abstract theory with concrete classroom tactics; conduct multi-trait validation (convergent, discriminant, criterion) to adjudicate. <cite id="8f33e454-3">Validity is a value proposition accumulating qualitative and quantitative evidence; scales are faithful mirrors of target constructs to the degree evidence supports them</cite> <cite id="637ee541-4">Validation is context-specific; acceptable fit and reliability in one context do not guarantee identical structures elsewhere</cite>.
</answer>

Title: A cross‐sectional study in college‐based nursing education: The influence of core self‐evaluation and career calling on study engagement in nursing undergraduates
Snippet: The questionnaires used in this study include five parts: The UWES-S, developed by Schaufeli, et al. (Schaufeli et al., 2002), is a widely used and well-validated tool for assessing student's study engagement. The UWES-S was translated into Chinese and validated by students by Fang et al. (Fang et al., 2008). In 2016, Chen (2016) briefed the scale into nine items and validated. The brief scale consisted of three dimensions: (a) vigour (3 items), (b) dedication (3 items) and (c) absorption (3 items). Each item was measured using a 5-point rating scale with responses ranging from 1 (completely oppose) to 5 (fully agree). For the present study, an average score was calculated from all nine items to indicate the level of engagement in higher education. Higher scores indicated more study engagement. In this study, the internal consistency reliability of the UWES-S-C measured by KR-20 was 0.899, showing excellent reliability. 

The CSES compiled by Judge et al. in 2003, and translated into Chinese by Du et al. in 2012. The CSES-C was tested on 386 undergraduate students, the results suggest that the Chinese vision scale was a valid measure (Du et al., 2012). This scale is characterized by a single dimension with 12 items in total. The Likert 5-level scoring method was adopted for each entry. A score of 1-5 indicated 'completely inconsistent to completely consistent,' and a higher score indicated a stronger CSE. The Cronbach's alpha coefficient of this scale in this study was 0.821. 

The Career Calling Scale for emerging adults was developed and validated by Praskova et al. (2015). It contains 15 items in three dimensions (other-oriented meaning, personal meaning and active engagement). This scale is a 6-point grading scale with endpoints of 1 = strongly disagree and 6 = strongly agree. With the author's consent, this scale was translated into Chinese by the researchers using the standard forward-backward procedure. Then, six experts (including two education professors, two psychology professors and two nursing professors) reviewed the Chinese vision scale.

Title: Development and initial validation of a creative self-efficacy scale for undergraduates: categorical confirmatory factor analysis and multidimensional item response theory
Snippet: To summarize, an example of developing and initially validating the intended interpretations of a CSE scale for undergraduates was provided by collecting and reporting three sources of validity evidence: (a) validity evidence based on scale content, (b) response processes, and (c) internal structure. Score reliability was also established by more robust methods (e.g., categorical omega and IRT-based marginal reliability) than those used in previous measures contributing to the methodological rigor of the present study compared to previously published studies. To conclude, the overall objective was to overcome the methodological and psychometric limitations noted through the literature review by developing a two-dimensional scale for measuring undergraduates' CSE, and initially validating its intended score interpretations using advanced psychometric models. Results supported the hypothesized two-dimensional factor structure with relatively high score reliability estimates.

Title: Intentional Learning Theory: Validating Its Measurement
Snippet: The purpose of this article was to present psychometric analysis of the extensive testing of the LOQ. Various sources of validity evidence were gathered and layered within an established validity model by Boateng et al. (2018). LOQ was found to satisfy the best practices of scale development and validation by exhibiting by a high degree of validity for the measurement of its intended construct, Intentional Learning. The instrument is firmly grounded in the theory of intentional learning and was composed and reviewed by qualified subject matter experts (SMEs). Under Phase Two, the data resulting from administration of the LOQ was subjected to pilot testing with various groups, statistical data reduction (principal components analysis), and item quality studies, evaluating endorseability, and discrimination. Finally, Phase Three yielded evidence supporting the LOQ as a single unitary construct, exhibiting a high degree of reliability (using two indices), and consistent measurement with similar and related constructs.

Title: Boy–Girl Differences in Pictorial Verbal Learning in Students Aged 8–12 Years and the Influence of Parental Education
Snippet: Intentional learning is of key importance for the acquisition of new information and for academic performance. The process of intentional learning can typically be described as having the purpose of learning information and committing it to one's memory (Thomas and Rohwer, 1986;Lezak et al., 2012;Hampshire et al., 2016). This is different from incidental learning, which is the accidental learning of information while actually concentrating on other information (Thomas and Rohwer, 1986;Lezak et al., 2012;Hampshire et al., 2016;Ahmed, 2017;Kontaxopoulou et al., 2017). The ability of intentional learning typically improves with experience and with age (Meijer et al., 2006(Meijer et al., , 2007;;Meijs et al., 2013Meijs et al., , 2016;;Blachstein and Vakil, 2016). It appears that there are major individual differences in the pace at which intentional learning develops at the end of childhood and the beginning of adolescence (Meijer et al., 2007;Jolles, 2016;Meijs et al., 2016;Juraska and Willing, 2017). 

Individual differences in intentional learning performance may contribute to individual variations in the ability to acquire and consolidate new information at school, as well as in learning motivation and school achievement. Examples of intentional learning at school is when students have to learn lists of words that belong to a new language and when they have to learn lists of conjugations of verbs. Another example of intentional learning at school is when new mathematical rules and multiplication tables need to be learned. Students with poor intentional learning ability may experience profound difficulties with learning lists of new words, conjugations of verbs as well as with learning new mathematical rules and lists of tables. This may negatively affect their language and mathematic performance as well as their learning motivation (Lawrence et al., 2015). It is therefore of importance to find out whether students are characterized by individual differences in intentional learning performance, and whether there are external factors that contribute to these individual differences. Identification of external factors could allow early detection of those individuals who are at risk of poor intentional learning performance, and thus also for problems with learning at school.

Title: Intentional Learning Theory: Validating Its Measurement
Snippet: The purpose of this article is to describe and analyze the psychometric properties of the Learning Orientation Questionnaire (LOQ), which have not been previously published. Psychometric validation involves the accumulation of proper empirical evidence to confirm measurement of the intended construct, and to justify the intended uses of the scales. LOQ is based upon the intentional learning theory, which is a comprehensive, holistic learning theory. Through the expertise of the LOQ’s developer, educational researcher, and psychometrician, this article presents evidence of LOQ’s reliability and validity according to published best practices for scale development and validation. LOQ is a reliable and valid instrument determining where learners fall along the learning orientation continuum. Education researchers can use this information to support learners to move upward on the learning orientation continuum, improving their inclination to learn, high-order thinking, and life-long learning.

Acceptable goodness of fit was claimed pointing to a theoretically sound structure for the two MSLQ scales. The original student populations for MSLQ development and validation were primarily consisted of undergraduate college students majoring in 14 subjects in the United States [22,3]. However, the concepts of selfregulated learning and the identification of suitable measures are likely to be equally beneficial in supporting medical students [24][25][26]. In this study, we adapted all 81 items from the original MSLQ with minor changes suitable for the clinical clerkship context. 

Although previous data on MSLQ's reliability and validity suggest it to be a reasonably valid tool for assessing SRL in medical education [27] validity is context-specific [28], and there are compelling reasons to explore how it operates within the population of clinical clerkship students. Despite its extensive use in medical education context with pre-clinical [26,[29][30][31][32][33][34][35][36], clinical [37][38][39][40], and postgraduate learners or residents [27,41], there is scarcity in research reporting MSLQ validation in clinical clerkship context. We found only 2 studies in the recent past that tried to validate MSLQ with clinical years students, that too used either a part of MSLQ or a shortened version. Dayel et al. [42] validated only Motivation scale of MSLQ in clinical years students and found satisfactory internal consistency but unsatisfactory model fit of Motivation scale for the specific context of Saudi Arabian medical students. Moreover, their sample consisted of only male students, thus raising further concerns over validation results. Fakhri et al. [38] validated a 32-item modified version of MSLQ, to measure reflection among clinical years students in Iran. Cook et al. [27] validated only Motivation scale with 120 residents and found a borderline fit with the theoretical framework, suggesting a five-factor Motivation scale without removing any items.

Title: Intentional Learning Theory: Validating Its Measurement
Snippet: Just as the development of the LOQ is an ongoing process, validation evidence collection is a continuous process. This is because, among other things, the LOQ constructs are theoretical abstractions embedded in theoretical frameworks that are greatly influenced by continuing developments in the neurosciences. Nonetheless, the findings provided herein substantiate the use of LOQ. LOQ as a valid measure will allow education researchers to determine where learners fall along the learning orientation continuum (transforming, performing, conforming, or resistant learners). According to their learning orientation, strategies to support the learners and improve their inclination to learn can be developed, such as customizing the learning environment to the learner's learning orientation which can have significant, positive influence on learner satisfaction and efficacy (Martinez, 1999a(Martinez, , 1999)). Future research should examine the impact of these changes on the learner's performance. 

Additionally, research should continue to test the LOQ's psychometric properties as well as examining how intentional learning impacts health professionals' learning in practical settings, filled with emotional experiences. According to Mollman and Candela (2018), the outcomes of intentional learning are high-order thinking and life-long learning which are vital skills for health professionals who must apply their knowledge to distinct patient situations. Well-developed and validated instruments are essential to understanding and accurately measuring constructs in health, social, and behavioral science (Boateng et al., 2018) but scale development is a complicated, multifaceted, and nonlinear process. Validity is not expressed as binary state (valid/invalid) but rather in degrees, as spectra amongst many different facets. The best of measurement scales accumulate a body of evidence, comprising both qualitative and quantitative elements, which supports and substantiates the computation and usage of scores. A validity argument is essentially a value proposition for the measurement instrument as a faithful ''mirror'' of the target construct, substantiating whether the scale is a trustworthy indicator of a quantifiable, and real attribute in the world.

snippet.text: The purpose of this article is to describe and analyze the psychometric properties of the Learning Orientation Questionnaire (LOQ), which have not been previously published. Psychometric validation involves the accumulation of proper empirical evidence to confirm measurement of the intended construct, and to justify the intended uses of the scales. LOQ is based upon the intentional learning theory, which is a comprehensive, holistic learning theory. Through the expertise of the LOQ’s developer, educational researcher, and psychometrician, this article presents evidence of LOQ’s reliability and validity according to published best practices for scale development and validation. LOQ is a reliable and valid instrument determining where learners fall along the learning orientation continuum. Education researchers can use this information to support learners to move upward on the learning orientation continuum, improving their inclination to learn, high-order thinking, and life-long learning.

snippet.text:
Just as the development of the LOQ is an ongoing process, validation evidence collection is a continuous process. This is because, among other things, the LOQ constructs are theoretical abstractions embedded in theoretical frameworks that are greatly influenced by continuing developments in the neurosciences. Nonetheless, the findings provided herein substantiate the use of LOQ. LOQ as a valid measure will allow education researchers to determine where learners fall along the learning orientation continuum (transforming, performing, conforming, or resistant learners). According to their learning orientation, strategies to support the learners and improve their inclination to learn can be developed, such as customizing the learning environment to the learner's learning orientation which can have significant, positive influence on learner satisfaction and efficacy (Martinez, 1999a(Martinez, , 1999)). Future research should examine the impact of these changes on the learner's performance. 

Additionally, research should continue to test the LOQ's psychometric properties as well as examining how intentional learning impacts health professionals' learning in practical settings, filled with emotional experiences. According to Mollman and Candela (2018), the outcomes of intentional learning are high-order thinking and life-long learning which are vital skills for health professionals who must apply their knowledge to distinct patient situations. Well-developed and validated instruments are essential to understanding and accurately measuring constructs in health, social, and behavioral science (Boateng et al., 2018) but scale development is a complicated, multifaceted, and nonlinear process. Validity is not expressed as binary state (valid/invalid) but rather in degrees, as spectra amongst many different facets. The best of measurement scales accumulate a body of evidence, comprising both qualitative and quantitative elements, which supports and substantiates the computation and usage of scores. Title: Evaluating Psychosocial Mechanisms Underlying STEM Persistence in Undergraduates: Evidence of Impact from a Six-Day Pre–College Engagement STEM Academy Program
Snippet: We completed a three-part validation of the measures used for our instrument. Development and selection of measures was driven by the theoretical foundation described earlier and followed a careful review of the literature. The constructs focused on in this study reflect the primary aims of the SA program. To assess the psychometric properties of our measures, we conducted a three-part analysis in which we 1) examined the factorial validity of the measures using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), 2) examined the internal consistency (reliability) of the respective measures, and 3) examined whether the scale variables evidence criterion validity via significant associations with measures we expect them to correlate with, including intention to leave STEM. Given that the measures used in the present study were based on preestablished, validated, and reliable published measures, we expected our approach to sufficiently address our aims (for a similar strategy used to validate a new survey measure of networking in undergraduate research experiences, see Hanauer and Hatfull, 2015). To have the statistical power (i.e., with a large enough sample) to conduct a factor analysis, we examined psychometric properties of the measures using data combined from the initial SA (pre survey) and entire non-SA group samples. Note, comparisons between SA and non-SA students on the measures and on retention were conducted using only the matched comparison group (see Results). 

CFAs. We used Mplus, version 7.4 (Muthén and Muthén, 1998), to conduct CFA on the survey variables. Model fit was evaluated using comparative fit index (CFI; acceptable model fit = 0.90 or above; good model fit = 0.95 or above), and root-mean-square error of approximation (RMSEA; good model fit =.05 or below, with 0.07 as an upper limit of acceptability; see Hu and Bentler, 1999). We also report the chi-squared test of significance; however, due to the impact of sample size on chi-squared tests, the CFI and RMSEA criteria are preferable to evaluate model fit. 

A model in which the items from each measure were set to load on their respective latent factor was estimated.

Title: Psychometric Properties of the Science Self-Efficacy Scale for STEMM Undergraduates
Snippet: Studies have found that science self-efficacy corresponds with a higher likelihood of pursuing a researchfocused career for both undergraduate and graduate/doctoral students (Adedokun et al., 2013;Chemers et al., 2011;Estrada et al., 2011). Additionally, studies have examined the relationship between science self-efficacy and other psychosocial measures such as science identity (Chemers, 2006) to obtain a more complete understanding of students' scientific training trajectories (Estrada et al., 2011). 

Validation studies that conduct a thorough examination of the psychometric properties of a scale are important because they ensure that the scale measures the target concept and appropriately represents the characteristics of its intended audience (AERA et al., 2014). Clarity on whether the scale used in a study has well-established psychometric properties and whether the scale operates similarly in different subgroups of a population ultimately enhances the trustworthiness of the results and implications of studies that employ validated scales. 

The current study examines the psychometric properties of the Science Self-Efficacy Scale (SSES), initially developed by Chemers et al. (2011) with 10 items and adapted into a six-item scale by Estrada et al. (2011). This six-item scale was used in the Enhance Diversity Study (EDS), a program assessment examining biomedical research capacity-building initiatives at 11 higher education institutions across the United States. At the time of the EDS, the adapted six-item SSES had not yet been validated using a large, national sample of diverse undergraduate students. 

We conducted a comprehensive validation of the scale by examining (a) construct validity, which includes an analysis of reliability coefficients, fitting an item response theory model, and assessing measurement invariance of how the scale functions across various subgroups, such as gender and race/ethnicity; (b) dimensionality using a cross-validation approach; and (c) validity based on other related traits or outcomes. By employing an item response theory framework, we were able to examine the specific item characteristics of the SSES and its relationship to the science self-efficacy latent construct. The results of this validation study provide critical information for researchers, evaluators, faculty, and administrators involved in initiatives that aim to facilitate retention in scientific career training environments.

Title: Bored to Be Wild: How Boredom Is Related to Pre-Service Teachers’ Intention to Persist in Their Studies
Snippet: All analyses were performed on R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using the lavaan package [45]. We performed a mediation analysis with structural equation modeling (SEM) to test (1) how control and value predicted boredom, and (2) how boredom was related to the intention to persist at university. We hypothesized that (1) the more participants felt a lack of control and low in value, the higher their boredom and (2) the more intense their boredom, the lower their intention to persist. We further hypothesized that both control and value would be positively related to the intention to persist (see Figure 1). 

Intention to persist in the university was measured using the scale used by Neuville [23,44]. Intention to persist can be considered as a proximal measure of actual persistence [23]. This scale consists of eight items such as: "Even if I didn't pass this year, I would start the same studies all over again", and "With two months of hindsight, I am satisfied with my choice". Four items were reversed, such as, "If I had known at the beginning of the year what I know now, I would have made another study choice". The scale presented acceptable reliability (alpha = 0.85). Participants were asked to answer on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Title: The Influence of Microaffirmations on Undergraduate Persistence in Science Career Pathways
Snippet: The present studies aimed to advance the measurement and understanding of microaffirmation kindness cues and assessed how they related to historically underrepresented (HU) and historically overrepresented (HO) undergraduate student persistence in science-related career pathways. Study 1 developed and tested the dimensionality of a new Microaffirmations Scale. Study 2 confirmed the two-factor structure of the Microaffirmations Scale and demonstrated that the scale possessed measurement invariance across HU and HO students. Further, the scale was administered as part of a longitudinal design spanning 9 months, with results showing that students’ reported microaffirmations did not directly predict higher intentions to persist in science-related career pathways 9 months later. However, scientific self-efficacy and identity, measures of student integration into the science community, mediated this relationship. Overall, our results demonstrated that microaffirmations can be measured in an academic context and that these experiences have predictive value when they increase students’ integration into their science communities, ultimately resulting in greater intentions to persist 9 months later. Researchers and practitioners can use the Microaffirmations Scale for future investigations to increase understanding of the positive contextual factors that can ultimately help reduce persistence gaps in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics degree attainment.

This six-item scale was used in the Enhance Diversity Study (EDS), a program assessment examining biomedical research capacity-building initiatives at 11 higher education institutions across the United States. At the time of the EDS, the adapted six-item SSES had not yet been validated using a large, national sample of diverse undergraduate students. 

We conducted a comprehensive validation of the scale by examining (a) construct validity, which includes an analysis of reliability coefficients, fitting an item response theory model, and assessing measurement invariance of how the scale functions across various subgroups, such as gender and race/ethnicity; (b) dimensionality using a cross-validation approach; and (c) validity based on other related traits or outcomes. By employing an item response theory framework, we were able to examine the specific item characteristics of the SSES and its relationship to the science self-efficacy latent construct. The results of this validation study provide critical information for researchers, evaluators, faculty, and administrators involved in initiatives that aim to facilitate retention in scientific career training environments.

documents.title: Bored to Be Wild: How Boredom Is Related to Pre-Service Teachers’ Intention to Persist in Their Studies
documents.snippet:
All analyses were performed on R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using the lavaan package [45]. We performed a mediation analysis with structural equation modeling (SEM) to test (1) how control and value predicted boredom, and (2) how boredom was related to the intention to persist at university. We hypothesized that (1) the more participants felt a lack of control and low in value, the higher their boredom and (2) the more intense their boredom, the lower their intention to persist. We further hypothesized that both control and value would be positively related to the intention to persist (see Figure 1). 

Intention to persist in the university was measured using the scale used by Neuville [23,44]. Intention to persist can be considered as a proximal measure of actual persistence [23]. This scale consists of eight items such as: "Even if I didn't pass this year, I would start the same studies all over again", and "With two months of hindsight, I am satisfied with my choice". Four items were reversed, such as, "If I had known at the beginning of the year what I know now, I would have made another study choice". The scale presented acceptable reliability (alpha = 0.85). Participants were asked to answer on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

documents.title: The Influence of Microaffirmations on Undergraduate Persistence in Science Career Pathways
documents.snippet: The present studies aimed to advance the measurement and understanding of microaffirmation kindness cues and assessed how they related to historically underrepresented (HU) and historically overrepresented (HO) undergraduate student persistence in science-related career pathways. Study 1 developed and tested the dimensionality of a new Microaffirmations Scale. Study 2 confirmed the two-factor structure of the Microaffirmations Scale and demonstrated that the scale possessed measurement invariance across HU and HO students. Further, the scale was administered as part of a longitudinal design spanning 9 months, with results showing that students’ reported microaffirmations did not directly predict higher intentions to persist in science-related career pathways 9 months later. However, scientific self-efficacy and identity, measures of student integration into the science community, mediated this relationship. Overall, our results demonstrated that microaffirmations can be measured in an academic context and that these experiences have predictive value when they increase students’ integration into their science communities, ultimately resulting in greater intentions to persist 9 months later. Researchers and practitioners can use the Microaffirmations Scale for future investigations to increase understanding of the positive contextual factors that can ultimately help reduce persistence gaps in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics degree attainment.

attempts.answer:
Below are validated, psychometrically supported scales that operationalize “intentionality” at the institutional level for universities, grouped by domain. In each case, intentionality is operationalized through concrete indicators of strategic commitment (formal policy/strategy), resource allocation and organizational practices, staff/student engagement, and monitoring/learning mechanisms, with item-level dimensions and reliability/validity evidence.

Internationalisation of Higher Education (IHE)
- What they measure: Intentionality as the degree to which internationalisation is purposefully embedded into an institution’s mission, functions, and delivery, beyond checkbox compliance. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality and integration are conceptualised as purposeful embedding of internationalisation into HEIs’ purpose, functions, and delivery, with indicators designed to capture the intentional aspect</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Intentionality is framed as a road requiring tangible actions across curriculum, staffing, professional development, partnerships, and integration into teaching and research; the framework and indicators are recommended for institutional policy use</cite>.
- Operationalisation:
  - Indicators elicited via “yes/no” questions to detect presence of formal strategy, governance, and resourcing for IHE, and Likert-scaled items to gauge depth of integration across multiple indicators per dimension. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators of intentionality can be captured with binary ‘yes/no’ items, while integration is measured by Likert items where full integration requires multiple indicators (e.g., four) to be fulfilled</cite>.
  - Example institutional dimensions/dimensions: curriculum internationalisation, student/staff mobility, partnerships, professional development, governance oversight, monitoring and evaluation. <cite id="237da9bd-3">Integrating an international dimension demands curriculum change, student recruitment, staff development, and partnerships; isolated actions are insufficient without holistic institutional strategy</cite>.
- Psychometrics: The framework is presented as “fit for purpose” for institutional policy use, with guidance on weighting indicators and contextual adaptation. <cite id="237da9bd-0">The measurement framework and indicators are ‘fit for purpose’ to guide integration of IHE into policies and practices</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Equal weighting is suggested initially, but institutions may assign different weights to indicators; further research to calibrate weights by context is recommended</cite>.
- Related validated instrument: India Study Centre Questionnaire (ISCQ) to measure IHE level, with reliability and content validation procedures. <cite id="237da9bd-4">The ISCQ was constructed from literature-derived themes, pilot-tested, and reliability/validity assessed via retest and expert interviews</cite>.

Sustainability and SDGs in Higher Education
- What they measure: Institutional intentionality toward sustainability as prioritisation and enactment of SDG-aligned strategy, encompassing environmental, social, and governance dimensions, with stakeholder engagement and impact orientation. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">HEIs must prioritise sustainability principles as the core foundation of strategy and address SDG challenges across curricula, operations, and culture, engaging multiple stakeholders</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">An 18-item instrument with four SDG-related dimensions measures perceptions of sustainability activities and provides a roadmap for wellbeing and stakeholder trust</cite>.
- Operationalisation:
  - Instrument structure: Four dimensions with SDG-linked items covering environmental management, social and economic impact, governance/organisational practices, and stakeholder engagement. <cite id="fbb894a2-1">A four-dimensional instrument with 18 SDG-related items was proposed after correlation-based refinement</cite>.
  - Example items/indicators: eco-friendly practices, renewable energy adoption, carbon reduction, energy efficiency, waste reduction, curricula on climate/circular economy/CSR, student-centered sustainability education, intersectoral collaboration, transparency and monitoring. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Instruments emphasise eco-friendly practices, renewable energy, emissions reduction, energy efficiency, waste minimisation, and educational programming on climate, circular economy, and CSR</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Universities should balance technology with human development and assess technologies that enhance teaching and learning as part of sustainability strategy</cite>.
  - Stakeholder and governance focus: Organisational reputation, trust, identification/loyalty intentions, and internal governance mechanisms (politics, profession, organisation, knowledge, visibility) to translate intention into action. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Governance dimensions (politics, profession, organisation, knowledge, visibility) and stakeholder trust/loyalty are integral to SDG implementation’s impact</cite>.
- Psychometrics:
  - Content validity (Aiken’s V >0.89) and high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.937) for the 18-item scale; EFA/CFA supported four-factor structure. <cite id="fbb894a2-4">Aiken’s V exceeded 0.89 and Cronbach’s alpha was 0.937 for a 18-item instrument; EFA supported four variables (economic/social impact, human rights/gender, environment/work experience, social impact) with satisfactory internal consistency</cite>.
  - Cross-instrument validation: SDG implementation scales show validity/reliability via EFA/CFA/SEM and are used to benchmark institutional performance across social, economic, and environmental dimensions. <cite id="fbb894a2-2">An SDG measurement instrument adopted from prior work was valid and reliable for assessing SDGs implementation in HEIs</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-3">EFA and CFA via SEM validated the factor structure and reliability of SDG items in HEIs; SPC and Pareto/IPMA analyses supported strategic prioritisation and resource allocation</cite>.
- Broader sustainability governance perspective: Models and instruments explicitly link sustainability strategy to governance and inter-organisational collaboration, operationalising intentionality through policy, oversight, and accountability. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Sustainable models prioritise environmental management and enhance community relationships, with governance models, social innovation, and public participation embedded in ethical and sustainable principles</cite>.

Innovation and Entrepreneurship (Institutional Climate and Support)
- What they measure: Institutional intentionality toward innovation/entrepreneurship as a climate and culture of support, resource supply, freedom/idea-support/risk-taking, and leadership/organisational commitment that translate policy into practice. <cite id="b85e8609-0">An innovation climate scale operationalises commitment, positive relationships, shared views, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking with 13 items</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Climate for innovation is proxied by support for innovation and resource supply, with validated significant effects on organisational commitment and retention</cite>.
- Operationalisation:
  - Climate dimensions and items: Leadership commitment, resource provision, cross-departmental collaboration, freedom to innovate, peer support, and risk tolerance, typically captured via Likert items and aggregated to indices. <cite id="b85e8609-0">Climate includes commitment, relationships, shared view, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking; a 13-item scale with Cronach’s alpha ~0.80 was developed</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Support for innovation and resource supply emerge as key subdimensions of innovation climate with significant effects on commitment</cite>.
  - Institutional policy-to-practice linkage: Courses, training programs, incubation/mentoring, funding opportunities, and campus-wide entrepreneurial support ecosystems that signal and enable intentionality. <cite id="b85e8609-2">HEIs optimise entrepreneurial environments via entrepreneurial education courses and institutional support in response to national innovation/entrepreneurship policies</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-3">Validated instruments combine altruism, innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and sustainable entrepreneurship objective; construct validity via content, expert, and statistical validation was achieved</cite>.
- Psychometrics:
  - Internal consistency and construct validity: Innovation climate scales show high reliability (e.g., Cronbach’s alpha around 0.8–0.9) and validated factor structures; effects on organisational commitment and retention are substantiated. <cite id="b85e8609-0">Reliability coefficient for the 13-item climate scale was Cronbach’s alpha = 0.80, with face/content validity</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Climate for innovation significantly predicts organisational commitment (β≈0.34, p<0.001), and resource supply and support for innovation account for substantial variance</cite>.
  - Student-level sustainable entrepreneurial intention: Multi-construct instruments combine institutional support with individual traits and sustainability goals; validated through three-stage procedures (content/expert/construct validation). <cite id="b85e8609-3">A 27-item instrument combining altruism, innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and sustainable entrepreneurship objectives was validated via content, expert, and statistical validation</cite>.

Cross-cutting Governance and Strategic Commitment (Policy, Oversight, Monitoring)
- ASEAN Graduate Training and Skills Training (ASEAN-GTST) exemplar: While focused on technical/skills governance, the ASEAN-GTST instrument demonstrates how institutional intentionality is operationalised via formal mechanisms for policy, implementation, oversight, incentives, and monitoring/evaluation—features transferable to higher education intentionality frameworks. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Formal institutional mechanisms scales assess formulation (existence of norms), supervision (oversight effectiveness), and dissemination (communication/ideological reinforcement), with reverse-coded items and strong reliability (Cronbach’s α up to 0.946); higher scores reflect stronger formal regulation and identity with institutional rules</cite>.
- Practical translation into university settings: Intentionality at the institutional level is operationalised through:
  - Clear statements of vision/mission and written policies that embed sustainability, internationalisation, or innovation priorities. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators include formal strategy and policy integration into institutional purpose and delivery</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Four dimensions capture SDG-related activities and perceptions, supporting a roadmap for wellbeing and stakeholder trust</cite>.
  - Resource allocation (budgets, staff, facilities), incentives, and professional development to enable implementation. <cite id="237da9bd-3">Institutional intentionality requires professional development and partnerships, not isolated initiatives</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support for innovation are core to innovation climate and commitment</cite>.
  - Organisational practices and culture (cross-departmental collaboration, freedom/idea-support, sustainability practices) and stakeholder engagement (students, staff, external partners). <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Sustainability culture and stakeholder engagement, including trust and identification, are central to SDG-aligned intentionality</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-0">Innovation climate includes shared views, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking</cite>.
  - Monitoring, evaluation, and reporting (KPIs, SDG dashboards, periodic audits) to ensure sustained intention–action alignment. <cite id="fbb894a2-3">Structural equation modelling and control charts (SPC) with Pareto and Importance–Performance maps guide monitoring and prioritise improvements</cite>.

How to choose and use the right scale
- Match to institutional goal and governance context:
  - Use the IHE intentionality framework when assessing deliberate integration of internationalisation into strategy, curriculum, staffing, and partnerships. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators combine binary presence of strategies with Likert-based integration depth across multiple indicators</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">The framework recommends moving beyond ticking boxes to holistic integration</cite>.
  - Use SDG sustainability instruments when evaluating institutional commitment and performance across environmental, social, and governance priorities and engaging stakeholders. <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Four-dimensional 18-item SDG instrument captures perceptions of sustainability activities and produces a roadmap for wellbeing and trust</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-4">High content validity and internal consistency support reliable measurement</cite>.
  - Use innovation/entrepreneurship climate scales when diagnosing enabling conditions (support, resources, freedom) and leadership commitment that translate into innovation output and staff/student retention. <cite id="b85e8609-0">Climate scale dimensions (commitment, relationships, freedom, idea-support, risk-taking) provide a validated structure</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support significantly shape commitment and retention</cite>.
- Implementation tips:
  - Combine policy/strategy audits (document review) with staff/student surveys to capture both formal intentionality (policies, oversight) and realised climate/practice. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Formal mechanisms scales assess policy formulation, supervision, and dissemination, enabling binary audits of policy presence and oversight</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Perception-based instruments quantify institutional activities and stakeholder trust</cite>.
  - Pilot items to local context, test reliability (Cronbach’s alpha), and validate factor structure (EFA/CFA) before full deployment; use results to calibrate indicator weights and target interventions. <cite id="fbb894a2-4">EFA/CFA supported four-factor structure and high internal consistency; weights can be calibrated by context</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Equal weighting may be relaxed to reflect institutional priorities; further research to refine weights is advised</cite>.

Limitations and validation needs
- Domain specificity: Instruments are validated within their domains (IHE, SDGs, innovation climate), and may require recalibration or additional validation for cross-domain transfer. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators and integration measurement are tailored to internationalisation; equal weighting and contextual adaptation are recommended</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-2">SDG instruments were validated in specific HEI settings and support benchmarking, but context-specific refinement remains valuable</cite>.
- Intention-to-action gap: Self-report measures (e.g., climate scales) capture perceptions; pairing with policy/audit instruments helps close the gap between stated intentionality and enacted practice. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Formal mechanisms scales quantify policy formulation, supervision, and dissemination, complementing perception-based measures</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support are actionable levers that translate climate into commitment</cite>.
- Future validation: Seek cross-cultural and sectoral invariance (public/private, research vs. teaching-focused) and longitudinal validity linking intentionality measures to institutional outcomes (research/teaching quality, sustainability performance). <cite id="fbb894a2-3">SEM/CFA validity and SPC-based monitoring provide a basis for longitudinal evaluation and resource prioritisation</cite>.

Summary
- Validated institutional-level intentionality instruments for universities exist and are most commonly operationalised via multi-dimensional scales that combine formal policy/oversight indicators with organizational climate and practice items, plus monitoring/learning mechanisms. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality is operationalised through presence of strategy and depth of integration, measured by binary and Likert indicators</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Sustainability intentionality instruments capture SDG-aligned activities across four dimensions with strong reliability</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-0">Innovation climate scales operationalise leadership commitment, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking via validated items</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support underpin climate and drive organisational commitment and retention</cite>.
- Examples and how they operationalise intentionality:
  - Internationalisation at home: yes/no policy and integration indicators; Likert-based integration across curriculum, staffing, partnerships, and PD. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality indicators and integration measurement plan</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Holistic integration actions and policy use</cite>.
  - Sustainability (SDGs): four-domain 18-item instrument with items on eco-practices, education, governance, stakeholder trust; validated with Aiken’s V and Cronbach’s alpha. <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Four dimensions; roadmap and stakeholder trust</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-4">High content validity and internal consistency</cite>.
  - Innovation/entrepreneurship: 13- and 27-item instruments capturing climate/support/resources and sustainable entrepreneurial intention; validated via content/expert/statistical validation. <cite id="b85e8609-0">13-item climate scale with documented reliability</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-3">27-item instrument combining innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and sustainability objectives with three-stage validation</cite>.
  - Governance/oversight: formal mechanisms scales to audit policy formulation, supervision, and dissemination; strong reliability supports diagnosing institutional regulation capacity. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Three dimensions (formulation, supervision, dissemination) with reverse-coded items and Cronbach’s α up to 0.946</cite>.

These instruments collectively provide a practical pathway to measure institutional intentionality: audit formal strategy and governance, survey staff/students on climate and practices, and monitor outcomes with validated metrics, enabling universities to prioritise interventions where intentionality is weakest and impact is greatest. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality and integration frameworks guide institutional policy and practice</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-3">EFA/CFA/SEM-based validation and control-chart benchmarking support targeted improvement</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support for innovation drive commitment, informing prioritisation</cite>.

Snippet: A framework with measurable indicators is developed to assess the extent to which an internationalisation undertaking in HEIs is an intentional and integrated endeavour. It is noted that IHE is understood both at the institutional level, where the real process of internationalisation takes place, and national level, where policy, funding, programmes, and regulatory frameworks that influence IHE are decided (Knight, 2004). However, IHE at the national level is beyond the scope of this paper. It should also be noted that intentionality and integration are not mutually exclusive concepts; instead, one reinforces the other to the extent that some indicators can equally be relevant for both attributes. 

Indicators of the intentional aspect can be addressed with a 'yes' or 'no' answers, making the measurement and analysis straightforward. However, integration is not an easy concept as it is more of a process than a state or an event. It demands continuous improvement to optimally integrate it into a HEI's purpose, functions, and delivery. Due to the nature of integration, a Likert scale question is proposed to better capture the extent to which the process of internationalisation is integrated (NB: a particular factor/ component is said to be fully integrated when all four indicators are fulfilled; mostly integrated when three of the indicators are fulfilled; partially integrated when two of the indicators are fulfilled; barely integrated when one of the indicators is fulfilled; and is not integrated when none of the indicators is fulfilled). Table 1 provides a framework to measure intentional and integration aspects of internationalisation at the higher education institutions level.
