Snippet: The Formal Institutional Mechanisms Scale developed by Chen Shanping et al. [3] was employed to assess students' perceptions of the comprehensiveness of school regulatory frameworks and their effectiveness in regulating student behavior. The scale comprises three dimensions: institutional formulation, supervision, and dissemination. Institutional formulation assesses whether the school has established a clear, reasonable, and comprehensive system of behavioral norms, consisting of three issues (e.g., "The behavioral norms for students' physical conduct at my university are not well-established"). Institutional supervision evaluates the adequacy of supervision provided by the school, faculty, and other administrative personnel, consisting of six issues (e.g., "My university lacks oversight of deviant behavior in physical activities"). Institutional dissemination examines whether the university conducts adequate communication and ideological education regarding behavioral norms, consisting of three issues (e.g., "My university has publicized the norms of sports behavior"). All items within this dimension are scored in reverse. The 5-point scale of Likert was used for scoring, from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", from "1" to "5". The average score of each dimension constitutes the total score of the scale, and the higher the score, the higher the students' sense of identity with the formal school regulation. In this study, the Cronbach's α coefficients for all subscales ranged from 0.865 to 0.946. Confirmatory factor analysis results were as follows: χ²/df = 18.77, NFI = 0.96, CFI = 0.96, IFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.08, demonstrating good reliability and validity of the scale.

Title: Testing Models and Measurement Invariance of the Learning Gains Scale
Snippet: Extensive research in higher education consistently suggests that student engagement is strongly associated with desirable educational outcomes such as increased learning, persistence in college, and graduation [1,2]. A student's knowledge, skills, and dispositions at the end of his or her undergraduate years undoubtedly have much to do with where he or she stands upon entering the world of work. Researchers argue that a university should be measured by how much students gain while enrolled, rather than what is measured on an absolute scale [3,4]. Some students grow more than others during their university years. At present perhaps the biggest challenge for several higher education institutions and quality assurance agencies is trying to develop and validate quality assessment instruments to determine a robust approach to measuring learning outcomes in ways that are valid across cultures and languages, and across the diversity of institutional settings.

Theories largely developed and largely supported by research conducted with students at institutions in a certain higher education context are likely to fit students at those institutions better than students at institutions in other higher education contexts [5]. Some levels of distinctiveness and modifications have been suggested by validation studies of student engagement surveys when used for two years and four year college students [6]. There is also evidence that suggests structural modification for the student engagement scale when used in a single institution study as opposed to large scale study [7][8][9]. Regardless of this, however, in higher education research, development and validation of student engagement and self-reported gains scales and cross-cultural comparisons have been rarely studied [10]. The lack of evidence supporting the cultural validity of constructs such as self-reported gain has implications for the wider utilization of those educational constructs across different higher education systems allowing customization to fit with different circumstances.

The development and validation of a self-reported Learning Gains Scale that is suitable for a particular higher education setting is valuable in examining the cultural relevance of an established construct while at the same time, creating local conditions and imprints to maximize the benefits [11]. A deeper analysis of the psychometric properties of a measuring instrument can be investigated through analysis of measurement invariance across groups at several levels. While this is most wanted and needed, the actual practice needs careful, step-by-step analysis [12].

Snippet: Metaphorically speaking, intentionality is a road, integration is a vehicle, and instrumentality (which is beyond the scope of this paper) is a destination. Hence, HEIs' management needs to move beyond a simple ticking of the intentional boxes to successfully integrate IHE into the purposes, services, and functions of their HEIs. 

Integrating an international dimension into the teaching function demands a synergy between several initiatives. These include making the curriculum international, attracting international students, recruiting international staff, providing continuous professional development to local staff to enhance their international competencies, and creating international partnerships for internships and similar opportunities. Universities seem to have focused on the 'low hanging fruits'internationalising curriculum contents. However, an isolated focus on a particular aspect makes the integration difficult, and its result will not support producing students with global competencies. Hence, HEIs need to address all the issues holistically. 

While the real development of strategic and comprehensive internationalisation takes many years of manageable steps, it demands identifying impediments and taking tangible action to address them. If HEIs in Ethiopia aspire to maximise the benefits of IHE, integrating it into the higher education system is vital. In addition, the measure of success in IHE should move beyond short-term gains (funding from IHE partnerships) to improve the quality of education and research and make a meaningful contribution to society. 

The framework and associated indicators developed in this study for 'measuring intentionality and integration' were useful and 'fit for purpose'. We recommend that these be included in institutional policies as useful 'tools' for integrating IHE into policies and practices at the institutional level. However, the authors would like to suggest where further research might go from this study. In this regard, adopting the measurement criteria to respective contexts is one. In this study, all indicators of intentionality and integration have been given equal weight. In fact, some institutions may see a rationale in giving more value to some indicators than others. Future studies may focus on identifying the values different institutions give to each indicator so as to refine and adapt the framework to diverse contexts.

Title: Measurement of Internationalisation: Development of India Study Centre Questionnaire
Snippet: The India Study Centre Questionnaire (ISCQ) has been developed to measure the level of internationalisation of higher education (IHE) with reference to India at the India Study centres in China. The concept of IHE has been constructed on the basis of the significantly correlated themes that emerged from the academic research literatures (N=36). The correlation among the emergent themes (N=52) comprising the components of the IHE was tested on the basis of a text analysis. The themes were itemised in accordance with the Ontological or Existentialist, Phenomenological or Instrumentalist, Propositional or Imagistic approaches of conceptualisation with an intent to satisfy the Evaluative or Normative need of the theoretical framework of this study. The designed instrument (ISCQ) devised on the emergent themes was administered on the students (N=28) of India study centre of Peking University, Beijing to test the reliability and validity of the instrument. In order to test and retest the robust validity of the instrument (ISCQ) two more rounds of piloting the questionnaire would be required. Five extensive interviews were conducted with the faculties to validate the structure and content of the ISCQ. However, owing to politico-academic sensitivity, approaching the respondents would need formal consent from the authorities of the institutions in context. Interviews were conducted with five teachers of country specific study centres from prominent institutions.

Title: Developing an Instrument and Assessing SDGs Implementation in Indonesian Higher Education
Snippet: This study uses a questionnaire instrument to measure research variables. This study employs three sections of statistical techniques to comprehensively evaluate the implementation and role of higher education institutions in the sustainability agenda. 

(1) This study used SDGs measurement items referring to Aleixo et al. [2]. However, this study carefully selected and employed relevant measurement items specific to the higher education context. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) are utilized to assess the validity of the measurement items developed for evaluating the implementation of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in higher education institutions. These techniques allow for the examination of the underlying factors and the confirmation of the measurement tool's reliability and construct validity. 

EFA plays a crucial role in determining whether the selected measurement items align well with the anticipated factors, thereby indicating their suitability for effectively measuring the variable of interest. Subsequently, CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis) is utilized to validate and confirm the identified factor structure from EFA while assessing its compatibility with the collected data. CFA employs more rigorous criteria, providing formal evidence concerning the validity of the factor structure. In this study, Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was performed to conduct the CFA test, ensuring the robust evaluation of the measurement model's validity for the SDGs in higher education institutions. 

(2) Statistical process control (SPC) analysis and Pareto diagrams are employed to evaluate the level of implementation of the SDGs agendas in higher education institutions using the developed measurement instrument. SPC analysis provides a systematic approach to monitor and control the implementation process, while Pareto diagrams and Importance-Performance Map analysis (IPMA) offer visual representations of the relative importance and performance of different SDGs agendas. These techniques aid in identifying areas of improvement and prioritizing resources for effective implementation. (3) Importance-Performance Map Analysis is also conducted to provide insights into the essentiality and effectiveness by the effect of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) agendas for implementation in higher education institutions. This analysis allows for the identification of SDGs agendas that are both highly important and have a significant impact on the institution's sustainability performance. It provides valuable information for strategic decision-making and resource allocation. Hence, higher education institutions can gradually implement the SDGs agendas based on their importance and effectiveness.

Title: Navigating interconnected complexities: validation and reliability of an instrument for sustainable development of education 5.0
Snippet: Abstract Sustainability actions in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) profoundly affect students, employees and their communities. These aim at social and economic benefits for local communities. Sustainability must be measured, and its goals must be achieved as part of the university’s mission to impact the community significantly. This work provides the validation results for an instrument that assesses academicians’ perceptions of HEI sustainability activities. The study began with a preliminary investigation of 121 Mexican public HEI students. The scale dimensions were constructed and validated in three steps: (a) establishing a theoretical framework to identify the necessary dimensions, (b) content validation through the judgment of five experts and (c) factor analysis and determination of instrument internal consistency to establish its reliability. The validation yielded three main findings: Aiken’s V coefficient (>0.89) showed high content-based validity indicators. Also, Cronbach’s alpha was 0.937. The exploratory factor analysis (EFA) calculated correlation coefficients for the 18-item instrument. The four variables tested in the study (economic and social impact, human rights and gender perspective, environment and work experience and social impact) yielded satisfactory internal consistency. The research affirms a methodology to measure the progress of sustainability models for Education 5.0 using technologies and resources to maximize human well-being.

The population for the study is 1085 faculty members in public universities of the Isfahan. This study uses a stratified random sampling method to select 400 faculty members. Title: The Influence of Organizational Commitment in Climate for Innovation and Employee Retention Relationship: An Empirical Study in Higher Education Institutions
Snippet: In this research, employee retention was predicted by climate for innovation at f² value 0.001, while organizational commitment at the f² value of 0.607. In addition, organizational commitment was predicted by climate for innovation at the f² value of 0.122. According to Cohen (1988), the f² value of 0.001 was less than a small threshold value of 0.02. On another note, the f² value of 0.122 was indicated to be higher than the medium threshold value of 0.15, whereas the f² value of 0.607 was revealed to be higher than a large threshold value of 0.35. 

The present research validated strong significant effect of climate for innovation represented by (β=0.342, t=7.516, p<0.001) on organizational commitment of academics in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). This finding broadly supports the work of established studies in this area. Hence, climate for innovation was found to be important to ensure the commitment of the academics in their profession. 

Referring to Table 9, strong significant effect of organizational commitment on employee retention was also confirmed (β=0.63; t-statistic=16.632, p<0.001). As supported by a well-established stream of research rooted in SET, employees' commitment to the organization was revealed to be derived from their perceptions of the employers' commitment in supporting them, or concerning the perception of employees regarding the same reflection from the part of organization (Hutchison and Garstka, 1996). Hence, committed employees who are not looking for employment elsewhere will remain longer with a positive perception about the organization (Eshiteti et al., 2013) and will be inclined to exhibit more positivity on-the-job behaviors (Harrison et al., 2006). 

It is clear that the present study has validated the insignificant association of climate for innovation on employee retention in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). On top of that, climate for innovation was measured through the two aspects of support for innovation and resource supply and proven to be important to climate for innovation at the significant weightage of β=0.751; t-statistic=11.971 and β=0.423; t-value=5.449, respectively.

Title: Gender-based differences in the relationships among proactive personality, perceived entrepreneurial support and entrepreneurial intention of Chinese private college students: A moderated mediation model
Snippet: Entrepreneurship and innovation have become mainstream of the economic and social reforms with the momentum of economic development and prosperity. In recent years, entrepreneurship promotion initiatives have boomed locally and globally. In 2015, Chinese government issued a nationwide entrepreneurship and innovation policy to stimulate mass creativity, increase employment, and promote vertical social mobility and social equality. Higher education institutions act as the engines of socioeconomic development, and college students are the driving force of entrepreneurship. To stimulate the entrepreneurial vitality and obtain fuller and high-quality employment for college students, Chinese state council introduced the Guidance on Further Supporting Innovation and Entrepreneurship of College Students in 2021, which placed great emphasis on building the entrepreneurship and innovative-oriented college students training model and optimizing college students' entrepreneurship environment. Higher education institutions at all levels in China have responded to the policies by setting up entrepreneurial education courses and providing institutional entrepreneurship support. 

Entrepreneurial intention refers to the self-acknowledged conviction and preparation for establishing a new business venture, adding value to an existing organization, or consciously planning to do so in the future (Wang et al., 2016). It has received considerable attention for positively influencing entrepreneurial behavior. In terms of entrepreneurial intention among college students, there is a negative relationship between the hierarchy of higher education institutions and entrepreneurial intention in China (Zhong et al., 2016). Accordingly, students in Chinese private colleges have stronger entrepreneurial intention because most private colleges are in the middle and lower layers of the hierarchical structure of Chinese higher education institutions. Although entrepreneurial intention is gaining increasing prominence, most studies on the entrepreneurial intention of Chinese higher education institutions focus on public colleges, which are prestigious and research-oriented higher education institutions. With the application orientation, Chinese private colleges can be keenly aware of market demand and take advantages of the combination of colleges and enterprises, which has not received sufficient attention in current entrepreneurship studies. Previous studies revealed Chinese college students' entrepreneurial intention and the predicted factors, such as attitude, personality, self-efficacy, sociodemographic exposure to supportive environment, and so on (Yang, 2013;Hu et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2019). Specifically, proactive personality traits and entrepreneurial support are prerequisites for entrepreneurship (Crant, 1996;Neneh, 2019a).

Below are validated, psychometrically supported scales that operationalize “intentionality” at the institutional level for universities, grouped by domain. In each case, intentionality is operationalized through concrete indicators of strategic commitment (formal policy/strategy), resource allocation and organizational practices, staff/student engagement, and monitoring/learning mechanisms, with item-level dimensions and reliability/validity evidence.

Internationalisation of Higher Education (IHE)
- What they measure: Intentionality as the degree to which internationalisation is purposefully embedded into an institution’s mission, functions, and delivery, beyond checkbox compliance. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality and integration are conceptualised as purposeful embedding of internationalisation into HEIs’ purpose, functions, and delivery, with indicators designed to capture the intentional aspect</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Intentionality is framed as a road requiring tangible actions across curriculum, staffing, professional development, partnerships, and integration into teaching and research; the framework and indicators are recommended for institutional policy use</cite>.
- Operationalisation:
  - Indicators elicited via “yes/no” questions to detect presence of formal strategy, governance, and resourcing for IHE, and Likert-scaled items to gauge depth of integration across multiple indicators per dimension. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators of intentionality can be captured with binary ‘yes/no’ items, while integration is measured by Likert items where full integration requires multiple indicators (e.g., four) to be fulfilled</cite>.
  - Example institutional dimensions/dimensions: curriculum internationalisation, student/staff mobility, partnerships, professional development, governance oversight, monitoring and evaluation. <cite id="237da9bd-3">Integrating an international dimension demands curriculum change, student recruitment, staff development, and partnerships; isolated actions are insufficient without holistic institutional strategy</cite>.
- Psychometrics: The framework is presented as “fit for purpose” for institutional policy use, with guidance on weighting indicators and contextual adaptation. <cite id="237da9bd-0">The measurement framework and indicators are ‘fit for purpose’ to guide integration of IHE into policies and practices</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Equal weighting is suggested initially, but institutions may assign different weights to indicators; further research to calibrate weights by context is recommended</cite>.
- Related validated instrument: India Study Centre Questionnaire (ISCQ) to measure IHE level, with reliability and content validation procedures. <cite id="237da9bd-4">The ISCQ was constructed from literature-derived themes, pilot-tested, and reliability/validity assessed via retest and expert interviews</cite>.

Sustainability and SDGs in Higher Education
- What they measure: Institutional intentionality toward sustainability as prioritisation and enactment of SDG-aligned strategy, encompassing environmental, social, and governance dimensions, with stakeholder engagement and impact orientation. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">HEIs must prioritise sustainability principles as the core foundation of strategy and address SDG challenges across curricula, operations, and culture, engaging multiple stakeholders</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">An 18-item instrument with four SDG-related dimensions measures perceptions of sustainability activities and provides a roadmap for wellbeing and stakeholder trust</cite>.
- Operationalisation:
  - Instrument structure: Four dimensions with SDG-linked items covering environmental management, social and economic impact, governance/organisational practices, and stakeholder engagement. <cite id="fbb894a2-1">A four-dimensional instrument with 18 SDG-related items was proposed after correlation-based refinement</cite>.
  - Example items/indicators: eco-friendly practices, renewable energy adoption, carbon reduction, energy efficiency, waste reduction, curricula on climate/circular economy/CSR, student-centered sustainability education, intersectoral collaboration, transparency and monitoring. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Instruments emphasise eco-friendly practices, renewable energy, emissions reduction, energy efficiency, waste minimisation, and educational programming on climate, circular economy, and CSR</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Universities should balance technology with human development and assess technologies that enhance teaching and learning as part of sustainability strategy</cite>.
  - Stakeholder and governance focus: Organisational reputation, trust, identification/loyalty intentions, and internal governance mechanisms (politics, profession, organisation, knowledge, visibility) to translate intention into action. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Governance dimensions (politics, profession, organisation, knowledge, visibility) and stakeholder trust/loyalty are integral to SDG implementation’s impact</cite>.
- Psychometrics:
  - Content validity (Aiken’s V >0.89) and high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.937) for the 18-item scale; EFA/CFA supported four-factor structure. <cite id="fbb894a2-4">Aiken’s V exceeded 0.89 and Cronbach’s alpha was 0.937 for a 18-item instrument; EFA supported four variables (economic/social impact, human rights/gender, environment/work experience, social impact) with satisfactory internal consistency</cite>.
  - Cross-instrument validation: SDG implementation scales show validity/reliability via EFA/CFA/SEM and are used to benchmark institutional performance across social, economic, and environmental dimensions. <cite id="fbb894a2-2">An SDG measurement instrument adopted from prior work was valid and reliable for assessing SDGs implementation in HEIs</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-3">EFA and CFA via SEM validated the factor structure and reliability of SDG items in HEIs; SPC and Pareto/IPMA analyses supported strategic prioritisation and resource allocation</cite>.
- Broader sustainability governance perspective: Models and instruments explicitly link sustainability strategy to governance and inter-organisational collaboration, operationalising intentionality through policy, oversight, and accountability. <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Sustainable models prioritise environmental management and enhance community relationships, with governance models, social innovation, and public participation embedded in ethical and sustainable principles</cite>.

Innovation and Entrepreneurship (Institutional Climate and Support)
- What they measure: Institutional intentionality toward innovation/entrepreneurship as a climate and culture of support, resource supply, freedom/idea-support/risk-taking, and leadership/organisational commitment that translate policy into practice. <cite id="b85e8609-0">An innovation climate scale operationalises commitment, positive relationships, shared views, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking with 13 items</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Climate for innovation is proxied by support for innovation and resource supply, with validated significant effects on organisational commitment and retention</cite>.
- Operationalisation:
  - Climate dimensions and items: Leadership commitment, resource provision, cross-departmental collaboration, freedom to innovate, peer support, and risk tolerance, typically captured via Likert items and aggregated to indices. <cite id="b85e8609-0">Climate includes commitment, relationships, shared view, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking; a 13-item scale with Cronach’s alpha ~0.80 was developed</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Support for innovation and resource supply emerge as key subdimensions of innovation climate with significant effects on commitment</cite>.
  - Institutional policy-to-practice linkage: Courses, training programs, incubation/mentoring, funding opportunities, and campus-wide entrepreneurial support ecosystems that signal and enable intentionality. <cite id="b85e8609-2">HEIs optimise entrepreneurial environments via entrepreneurial education courses and institutional support in response to national innovation/entrepreneurship policies</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-3">Validated instruments combine altruism, innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and sustainable entrepreneurship objective; construct validity via content, expert, and statistical validation was achieved</cite>.
- Psychometrics:
  - Internal consistency and construct validity: Innovation climate scales show high reliability (e.g., Cronbach’s alpha around 0.8–0.9) and validated factor structures; effects on organisational commitment and retention are substantiated. <cite id="b85e8609-0">Reliability coefficient for the 13-item climate scale was Cronbach’s alpha = 0.80, with face/content validity</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Climate for innovation significantly predicts organisational commitment (β≈0.34, p<0.001), and resource supply and support for innovation account for substantial variance</cite>.
  - Student-level sustainable entrepreneurial intention: Multi-construct instruments combine institutional support with individual traits and sustainability goals; validated through three-stage procedures (content/expert/construct validation). <cite id="b85e8609-3">A 27-item instrument combining altruism, innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and sustainable entrepreneurship objectives was validated via content, expert, and statistical validation</cite>.

Cross-cutting Governance and Strategic Commitment (Policy, Oversight, Monitoring)
- ASEAN Graduate Training and Skills Training (ASEAN-GTST) exemplar: While focused on technical/skills governance, the ASEAN-GTST instrument demonstrates how institutional intentionality is operationalised via formal mechanisms for policy, implementation, oversight, incentives, and monitoring/evaluation—features transferable to higher education intentionality frameworks. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Formal institutional mechanisms scales assess formulation (existence of norms), supervision (oversight effectiveness), and dissemination (communication/ideological reinforcement), with reverse-coded items and strong reliability (Cronbach’s α up to 0.946); higher scores reflect stronger formal regulation and identity with institutional rules</cite>.
- Practical translation into university settings: Intentionality at the institutional level is operationalised through:
  - Clear statements of vision/mission and written policies that embed sustainability, internationalisation, or innovation priorities. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators include formal strategy and policy integration into institutional purpose and delivery</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Four dimensions capture SDG-related activities and perceptions, supporting a roadmap for wellbeing and stakeholder trust</cite>.
  - Resource allocation (budgets, staff, facilities), incentives, and professional development to enable implementation. <cite id="237da9bd-3">Institutional intentionality requires professional development and partnerships, not isolated initiatives</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support for innovation are core to innovation climate and commitment</cite>.
  - Organisational practices and culture (cross-departmental collaboration, freedom/idea-support, sustainability practices) and stakeholder engagement (students, staff, external partners). <cite id="fbb894a2-0">Sustainability culture and stakeholder engagement, including trust and identification, are central to SDG-aligned intentionality</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-0">Innovation climate includes shared views, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking</cite>.
  - Monitoring, evaluation, and reporting (KPIs, SDG dashboards, periodic audits) to ensure sustained intention–action alignment. <cite id="fbb894a2-3">Structural equation modelling and control charts (SPC) with Pareto and Importance–Performance maps guide monitoring and prioritise improvements</cite>.

How to choose and use the right scale
- Match to institutional goal and governance context:
  - Use the IHE intentionality framework when assessing deliberate integration of internationalisation into strategy, curriculum, staffing, and partnerships. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators combine binary presence of strategies with Likert-based integration depth across multiple indicators</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">The framework recommends moving beyond ticking boxes to holistic integration</cite>.
  - Use SDG sustainability instruments when evaluating institutional commitment and performance across environmental, social, and governance priorities and engaging stakeholders. <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Four-dimensional 18-item SDG instrument captures perceptions of sustainability activities and produces a roadmap for wellbeing and trust</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-4">High content validity and internal consistency support reliable measurement</cite>.
  - Use innovation/entrepreneurship climate scales when diagnosing enabling conditions (support, resources, freedom) and leadership commitment that translate into innovation output and staff/student retention. <cite id="b85e8609-0">Climate scale dimensions (commitment, relationships, freedom, idea-support, risk-taking) provide a validated structure</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support significantly shape commitment and retention</cite>.
- Implementation tips:
  - Combine policy/strategy audits (document review) with staff/student surveys to capture both formal intentionality (policies, oversight) and realised climate/practice. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Formal mechanisms scales assess policy formulation, supervision, and dissemination, enabling binary audits of policy presence and oversight</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Perception-based instruments quantify institutional activities and stakeholder trust</cite>.
  - Pilot items to local context, test reliability (Cronbach’s alpha), and validate factor structure (EFA/CFA) before full deployment; use results to calibrate indicator weights and target interventions. <cite id="fbb894a2-4">EFA/CFA supported four-factor structure and high internal consistency; weights can be calibrated by context</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Equal weighting may be relaxed to reflect institutional priorities; further research to refine weights is advised</cite>.

Limitations and validation needs
- Domain specificity: Instruments are validated within their domains (IHE, SDGs, innovation climate), and may require recalibration or additional validation for cross-domain transfer. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Indicators and integration measurement are tailored to internationalisation; equal weighting and contextual adaptation are recommended</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-2">SDG instruments were validated in specific HEI settings and support benchmarking, but context-specific refinement remains valuable</cite>.
- Intention-to-action gap: Self-report measures (e.g., climate scales) capture perceptions; pairing with policy/audit instruments helps close the gap between stated intentionality and enacted practice. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Formal mechanisms scales quantify policy formulation, supervision, and dissemination, complementing perception-based measures</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support are actionable levers that translate climate into commitment</cite>.
- Future validation: Seek cross-cultural and sectoral invariance (public/private, research vs. teaching-focused) and longitudinal validity linking intentionality measures to institutional outcomes (research/teaching quality, sustainability performance). <cite id="fbb894a2-3">SEM/CFA validity and SPC-based monitoring provide a basis for longitudinal evaluation and resource prioritisation</cite>.

Summary
- Validated institutional-level intentionality instruments for universities exist and are most commonly operationalised via multi-dimensional scales that combine formal policy/oversight indicators with organizational climate and practice items, plus monitoring/learning mechanisms. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality is operationalised through presence of strategy and depth of integration, measured by binary and Likert indicators</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Sustainability intentionality instruments capture SDG-aligned activities across four dimensions with strong reliability</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-0">Innovation climate scales operationalise leadership commitment, freedom, idea-support, and risk-taking via validated items</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support underpin climate and drive organisational commitment and retention</cite>.
- Examples and how they operationalise intentionality:
  - Internationalisation at home: yes/no policy and integration indicators; Likert-based integration across curriculum, staffing, partnerships, and PD. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality indicators and integration measurement plan</cite> <cite id="237da9bd-3">Holistic integration actions and policy use</cite>.
  - Sustainability (SDGs): four-domain 18-item instrument with items on eco-practices, education, governance, stakeholder trust; validated with Aiken’s V and Cronbach’s alpha. <cite id="fbb894a2-1">Four dimensions; roadmap and stakeholder trust</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-4">High content validity and internal consistency</cite>.
  - Innovation/entrepreneurship: 13- and 27-item instruments capturing climate/support/resources and sustainable entrepreneurial intention; validated via content/expert/statistical validation. <cite id="b85e8609-0">13-item climate scale with documented reliability</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-3">27-item instrument combining innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and sustainability objectives with three-stage validation</cite>.
  - Governance/oversight: formal mechanisms scales to audit policy formulation, supervision, and dissemination; strong reliability supports diagnosing institutional regulation capacity. <cite id="237da9bd-1">Three dimensions (formulation, supervision, dissemination) with reverse-coded items and Cronbach’s α up to 0.946</cite>.

These instruments collectively provide a practical pathway to measure institutional intentionality: audit formal strategy and governance, survey staff/students on climate and practices, and monitor outcomes with validated metrics, enabling universities to prioritise interventions where intentionality is weakest and impact is greatest. <cite id="237da9bd-0">Intentionality and integration frameworks guide institutional policy and practice</cite> <cite id="fbb894a2-3">EFA/CFA/SEM-based validation and control-chart benchmarking support targeted improvement</cite> <cite id="b85e8609-1">Resource supply and support for innovation drive commitment, informing prioritisation</cite>.</answer>

Title: Internationalisation of Higher Education in Ethiopia: A Strategic Process?
Snippet: A framework with measurable indicators is developed to assess the extent to which an internationalisation undertaking in HEIs is an intentional and integrated endeavour. It is noted that IHE is understood both at the institutional level, where the real process of internationalisation takes place, and national level, where policy, funding, programmes, and regulatory frameworks that influence IHE are decided (Knight, 2004). However, IHE at the national level is beyond the scope of this paper. It should also be noted that intentionality and integration are not mutually exclusive concepts; instead, one reinforces the other to the extent that some indicators can equally be relevant for both attributes. 

Indicators of the intentional aspect can be addressed with a 'yes' or 'no' answers, making the measurement and analysis straightforward. However, integration is not an easy concept as it is more of a process than a state or an event. It demands continuous improvement to optimally integrate it into a HEI's purpose, functions, and delivery. Due to the nature of integration, a Likert scale question is proposed to better capture the extent to which the process of internationalisation is integrated (NB: a particular factor/ component is said to be fully integrated when all four indicators are fulfilled; mostly integrated when three of the indicators are fulfilled; partially integrated when two of the indicators are fulfilled; barely integrated when one of the indicators is fulfilled; and is not integrated when none of the indicators is fulfilled). Table 1 provides a framework to measure intentional and integration aspects of internationalisation at the higher education institutions level.

Title: The impact of peer effects on college students’ sports normative behavior intention: a moderated mediation model
Snippet: The Formal Institutional Mechanisms Scale developed by Chen Shanping et al. [3] was employed to assess students' perceptions of the comprehensiveness of school regulatory frameworks and their effectiveness in regulating student behavior. The scale comprises three dimensions: institutional formulation, supervision, and dissemination. Institutional formulation assesses whether the school has established a clear, reasonable, and comprehensive system of behavioral norms, consisting of three issues (e.g., "The behavioral norms for students' physical conduct at my university are not well-established"). Institutional supervision evaluates the adequacy of supervision provided by the school, faculty, and other administrative personnel, consisting of six issues (e.g., "My university lacks oversight of deviant behavior in physical activities"). Institutional dissemination examines whether the university conducts adequate communication and ideological education regarding behavioral norms, consisting of three issues (e.g., "My university has publicized the norms of sports behavior"). All items within this dimension are scored in reverse. The 5-point scale of Likert was used for scoring, from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", from "1" to "5". The average score of each dimension constitutes the total score of the scale, and the higher the score, the higher the students' sense of identity with the formal school regulation. In this study, the Cronbach's α coefficients for all subscales ranged from 0.865 to 0.946. Confirmatory factor analysis results were as follows: χ²/df = 18.77, NFI = 0.96, CFI = 0.96, IFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.08, demonstrating good reliability and validity of the scale.

Title: Testing Models and Measurement Invariance of the Learning Gains Scale
Snippet: Extensive research in higher education consistently suggests that student engagement is strongly associated with desirable educational outcomes such as increased learning, persistence in college, and graduation [1,2]. A student's knowledge, skills, and dispositions at the end of his or her undergraduate years undoubtedly have much to do with where he or she stands upon entering the world of work. Researchers argue that a university should be measured by how much students gain while enrolled, rather than what is measured on an absolute scale [3,4]. Some students grow more than others during their university years. At present perhaps the biggest challenge for several higher education institutions and quality assurance agencies is trying to develop and validate quality assessment instruments to determine a robust approach to measuring learning outcomes in ways that are valid across cultures and languages, and across the diversity of institutional settings.

Theories largely developed and largely supported by research conducted with students at institutions in a certain higher education context are likely to fit students at those institutions better than students at institutions in other higher education contexts [5]. Some levels of distinctiveness and modifications have been suggested by validation studies of student engagement surveys when used for two years and four year college students [6]. There is also evidence that suggests structural modification for the student engagement scale when used in a single institution study as opposed to large scale study [7][8][9]. Regardless of this, however, in higher education research, development and validation of student engagement and self-reported gains scales and cross-cultural comparisons have been rarely studied [10]. Title: Internationalisation of Higher Education in Ethiopia: A Strategic Process?
Snippet: Metaphorically speaking, intentionality is a road, integration is a vehicle, and instrumentality (which is beyond the scope of this paper) is a destination. Hence, HEIs' management needs to move beyond a simple ticking of the intentional boxes to successfully integrate IHE into the purposes, services, and functions of their HEIs. 

Integrating an international dimension into the teaching function demands a synergy between several initiatives. These include making the curriculum international, attracting international students, recruiting international staff, providing continuous professional development to local staff to enhance their international competencies, and creating international partnerships for internships and similar opportunities. Universities seem to have focused on the 'low hanging fruits'internationalising curriculum contents. However, an isolated focus on a particular aspect makes the integration difficult, and its result will not support producing students with global competencies. Hence, HEIs need to address all the issues holistically. 

While the real development of strategic and comprehensive internationalisation takes many years of manageable steps, it demands identifying impediments and taking tangible action to address them. If HEIs in Ethiopia aspire to maximise the benefits of IHE, integrating it into the higher education system is vital. In addition, the measure of success in IHE should move beyond short-term gains (funding from IHE partnerships) to improve the quality of education and research and make a meaningful contribution to society. 

The framework and associated indicators developed in this study for 'measuring intentionality and integration' were useful and 'fit for purpose'. We recommend that these be included in institutional policies as useful 'tools' for integrating IHE into policies and practices at the institutional level. However, the authors would like to suggest where further research might go from this study. In this regard, adopting the measurement criteria to respective contexts is one. In this study, all indicators of intentionality and integration have been given equal weight. In fact, some institutions may see a rationale in giving more value to some indicators than others. Future studies may focus on identifying the values different institutions give to each indicator so as to refine and adapt the framework to diverse contexts.

Title: Measurement of Internationalisation: Development of India Study Centre Questionnaire
Snippet: The India Study Centre Questionnaire (ISCQ) has been developed to measure the level of internationalisation of higher education (IHE) with reference to India at the India Study centres in China. The concept of IHE has been constructed on the basis of the significantly correlated themes that emerged from the academic research literatures (N=36). The correlation among the emergent themes (N=52) comprising the components of the IHE was tested on the basis of a text analysis. The themes were itemised in accordance with the Ontological or Existentialist, Phenomenological or Instrumentalist, Propositional or Imagistic approaches of conceptualisation with an intent to satisfy the Evaluative or Normative need of the theoretical framework of this study. The designed instrument (ISCQ) devised on the emergent themes was administered on the students (N=28) of India study centre of Peking University, Beijing to test the reliability and validity of the instrument. In order to test and retest the robust validity of the instrument (ISCQ) two more rounds of piloting the questionnaire would be required. Five extensive interviews were conducted with the faculties to validate the structure and content of the ISCQ. However, owing to politico-academic sensitivity, approaching the respondents would need formal consent from the authorities of the institutions in context. Interviews were conducted with five teachers of country specific study centres from prominent institutions.

In addition, the measure of success in IHE should move beyond short-term gains (funding from IHE partnerships) to improve the quality of education and research and make a meaningful contribution to society. 

The framework and associated indicators developed in this study for 'measuring intentionality and integration' were useful and 'fit for purpose'. documents.title: Internationalisation of Higher Education in Ethiopia: A Strategic Process?
documents.snippet:
A framework with measurable indicators is developed to assess the extent to which an internationalisation undertaking in HEIs is an intentional and integrated endeavour. It is noted that IHE is understood both at the institutional level, where the real process of internationalisation takes place, and national level, where policy, funding, programmes, and regulatory frameworks that influence IHE are decided (Knight, 2004). However, IHE at the national level is beyond the scope of this paper. It should also be noted that intentionality and integration are not mutually exclusive concepts; instead, one reinforces the other to the extent that some indicators can equally be relevant for both attributes. 

Indicators of the intentional aspect can be addressed with a 'yes' or 'no' answers, making the measurement and analysis straightforward. However, integration is not an easy concept as it is more of a process than a state or an event. It demands continuous improvement to optimally integrate it into a HEI's purpose, functions, and delivery. Due to the nature of integration, a Likert scale question is proposed to better capture the extent to which the process of internationalisation is integrated (NB: a particular factor/ component is said to be fully integrated when all four indicators are fulfilled; mostly integrated when three of the indicators are fulfilled; partially integrated when two of the indicators are fulfilled; barely integrated when one of the indicators is fulfilled; and is not integrated when none of the indicators is fulfilled). Table 1 provides a framework to measure intentional and integration aspects of internationalisation at the higher education institutions level.

documents.snippet: The Formal Institutional Mechanisms Scale developed by Chen Shanping et al. [3] was employed to assess students' perceptions of the comprehensiveness of school regulatory frameworks and their effectiveness in regulating student behavior. The scale comprises three dimensions: institutional formulation, supervision, and dissemination. Institutional formulation assesses whether the school has established a clear, reasonable, and comprehensive system of behavioral norms, consisting of three issues (e.g., "The behavioral norms for students' physical conduct at my university are not well-established"). Institutional supervision evaluates the adequacy of supervision provided by the school, faculty, and other administrative personnel, consisting of six issues (e.g., "My university lacks oversight of deviant behavior in physical activities"). Institutional dissemination examines whether the university conducts adequate communication and ideological education regarding behavioral norms, consisting of three issues (e.g., "My university has publicized the norms of sports behavior"). All items within this dimension are scored in reverse. The 5-point scale of Likert was used for scoring, from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", from "1" to "5". The average score of each dimension constitutes the total score of the scale, and the higher the score, the higher the students' sense of identity with the formal school regulation. In this study, the Cronbach's α coefficients for all subscales ranged from 0.865 to 0.946. Confirmatory factor analysis results were as follows: χ²/df = 18.77, NFI = 0.96, CFI = 0.96, IFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.08, demonstrating good reliability and validity of the scale.

documents.title: Testing Models and Measurement Invariance of the Learning Gains Scale
documents.snippet:
Extensive research in higher education consistently suggests that student engagement is strongly associated with desirable educational outcomes such as increased learning, persistence in college, and graduation [1,2]. A student's knowledge, skills, and dispositions at the end of his or her undergraduate years undoubtedly have much to do with where he or she stands upon entering the world of work. Researchers argue that a university should be measured by how much students gain while enrolled, rather than what is measured on an absolute scale [3,4]. Some students grow more than others during their university years. At present perhaps the biggest challenge for several higher education institutions and quality assurance agencies is trying to develop and validate quality assessment instruments to determine a robust approach to measuring learning outcomes in ways that are valid across cultures and languages, and across the diversity of institutional settings.

Theories largely developed and largely supported by research conducted with students at institutions in a certain higher education context are likely to fit students at those institutions better than students at institutions in other higher education contexts [5]. Some levels of distinctiveness and modifications have been suggested by validation studies of student engagement surveys when used for two years and four year college students [6]. There is also evidence that suggests structural modification for the student engagement scale when used in a single institution study as opposed to large scale study [7][8][9]. Regardless of this, however, in higher education research, development and validation of student engagement and self-reported gains scales and cross-cultural comparisons have been rarely studied [10]. The lack of evidence supporting the cultural validity of constructs such as self-reported gain has implications for the wider utilization of those educational constructs across different higher education systems allowing customization to fit with different circumstances.

A deeper analysis of the psychometric properties of a measuring instrument can be investigated through analysis of measurement invariance across groups at several levels. While this is most wanted and needed, the actual practice needs careful, step-by-step analysis [12].

Title: Navigating interconnected complexities: validation and reliability of an instrument for sustainable development of education 5.0
Snippet: The generation of knowledge through applied research (Hamadi & El-Den, 2023) contends that for the desired change in education to occur, HEIs must prioritize sustainability principles as the core foundation of their strategy ( Zal _ enien _ e & Pereira, 2021) and address the challenges of sustainability and the SDGs outlined in the 2030 agenda (Pasara, 2021). This includes incorporating these ideas into various aspects such as curricula, operations and organizational culture and empowering the institution to exert a more substantial and advantageous impact as a crucial contributor in advancing sustainability. 

Including various efforts in the university context will create a new awareness within the institution through the active participation of a wide range of stakeholders, such as students, managers, external partners, university professors and researchers. In addition, this instrument suggests interconnections with diverse SDGs by each dimension; it offers a new perspective on how they are integrated within and outside HEIs (Figure 1). Greenland et al. (2023) created a six-dimensional sustainable development model with 37 SDG aspects relating to excellent education, peace, justice and strong institutions that require sustainability training to influence stakeholder behavior. Barta et al. (2023) created an instrument with key SDG dimensions like perceptions of environmental, social, and economic compliance, organizational reputation, trust, user-organization identification and loyalty intentions to examine how an educational institution's SDG implementation affects user perceptions and loyalty, including university employees and students. Bauer et al. (2018) proposed five governance dimensions: politics, profession, organization, knowledge and visibility. Sustainable models that prioritize environmental management and enhance community relationships are essential. HEIs, while focusing on these aspects, should also recognize their role in contributing to their respective communities' economic, social and cultural development. 

Moreover, conducting validity tests ensures the reliability and accuracy of the items for each dimension, allowing for confident and contextually appropriate application within specific educational settings. The application of this assessment instrument is valuable in gauging the level of proficiency in social entrepreneurship competency at the higher education level. The final instrument, detailed in Table 7, provides universities with a means to assess their sustainability initiatives comprehensively.

Title: Navigating interconnected complexities: validation and reliability of an instrument for sustainable development of education 5.0
Snippet: This study has important practical and research implications. HEIs must prioritize the development of a culture centered around sustainability. This involves adopting eco-friendly practices, supporting renewable energy, decreasing carbon emissions, encouraging sustainable transportation, improving energy efficiency in buildings, minimizing waste production and incorporating educational programs and curricula focusing on climate change, circular economy and corporate social responsibility. Additionally, universities should promote student-centered learning, emphasizing soft skills, ethics and awareness of social and environmental issues. It is essential to balance advanced technology and human development and assess the effectiveness of technologies that enhance teaching and learning. 

Given the scarcity of instruments that measure the maturity of sustainability in universities, especially in Mexico and Latin America, this research is particularly significant. Universities need to implement such measurements to comprehensively evaluate aspects contributing to sustainability. This instrument was developed by the Research for Challenges Group at Tecnol ogico de Monterrey and can be used by educational institutions, especially those in higher education. One challenge is establishing research institutions dedicated to advancing Education 5.0 with a focus on sustainability, as there are further ramifications associated with a technology-driven educational approach that prioritizes the welfare of humans and the environment. Furthermore, it is crucial to incorporate governance models, social innovation and public participation within ethical and sustainable principles. Another essential characteristic is developing collaboration between the community, government and corporate sectors on sustainable projects that benefit all. This collaboration enhances the connections between education and society. 

This instrument is a valuable resource for decision-makers assessing university sustainability initiatives. Further research is needed to explore whether the dimensions proposed in this instrument sufficiently address institution-specific concerns based on their contexts and locations. Additionally, incorporating political, governmental and economic aspects of the institutional development environment could enhance the instrument by including more nuanced elements from adjacent areas. 

This study aimed to report the findings of a validated instrument designed to measure the perception of the academic community regarding the sustainability activities implemented by their HEIs. After three stages, the research allowed the proposal of a four-dimensional instrument with 18 SDG-related items. With this instrument, it is possible to produce a roadmap for the pursuit of wellbeing and easily integrate actions that impact society, gaining greater trust within the academic community and among external stakeholders. The instrument's dimensions were adjusted based on the correlation findings and are displayed in Table 7.

Title: Developing an Instrument and Assessing SDGs Implementation in Indonesian Higher Education
Snippet: The results of testing the research instrument adopted from previous studies by Aleixo et al. [2,5] and Tabucanon et al. [8] were valid and reliable in measuring the intended constructs. It has been found that all the indicators and questions in the research instrument were suitable for use. The findings indicate that the proposed measurement instrument for SDGs agendas is suitable for assessing the implementation of SDGs in higher education institutions. The instrument has been designed and tested to effectively measure the key aspects of SDGs implementation, allowing for a comprehensive assessment of progress and performance. 

By implementing this measurement instrument, higher education institutions can systematically evaluate their efforts in relation to the SDGs agendas. It provides a structured approach to assess various dimensions of sustainability development, including social, economic, and environmental aspects. The instrument allows for a comprehensive evaluation of the extent to which the institutions are aligned with and actively working towards achieving the SDGs. The instrument also facilitates benchmarking and comparisons with other institutions, fostering learning and collaboration in the pursuit of sustainable development. 

The second research objective aimed to assess the level of implementation of the 17 SDGs agendas in higher education institutions. This assessment provided valuable insights into the extent to which the SDGs agendas have been effectively implemented in these institutions. In conclusion, the findings of this study indicate that the implementation of the SDGs agendas in higher education institutions, specifically in private institutions under the Muhammadiyah organization, is positioned in the middle range. While there are notable achievements and efforts in implementing the SDGs, there is still room for improvement. 

The study reveals that certain SDGs have been prioritized and implemented with relatively good performance, while others may require further attention and strategic planning. The measurement and evaluation of tertiary institutions in Indonesia is carried out by the Higher Education Accreditation Board which is the Indonesian government's accreditation agency. Assessment indicators include nine criteria, namely vision, mission, goals and objectives; governance, governance and cooperation; student; human Resources; finance, facilities and infrastructure; education; study; community service; tridharma outcomes and achievements [36].

Title: Developing an Instrument and Assessing SDGs Implementation in Indonesian Higher Education
Snippet: This study uses a questionnaire instrument to measure research variables. This study employs three sections of statistical techniques to comprehensively evaluate the implementation and role of higher education institutions in the sustainability agenda. 

(1) This study used SDGs measurement items referring to Aleixo et al. [2]. However, this study carefully selected and employed relevant measurement items specific to the higher education context. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) are utilized to assess the validity of the measurement items developed for evaluating the implementation of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in higher education institutions. These techniques allow for the examination of the underlying factors and the confirmation of the measurement tool's reliability and construct validity. 

EFA plays a crucial role in determining whether the selected measurement items align well with the anticipated factors, thereby indicating their suitability for effectively measuring the variable of interest. Subsequently, CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis) is utilized to validate and confirm the identified factor structure from EFA while assessing its compatibility with the collected data. CFA employs more rigorous criteria, providing formal evidence concerning the validity of the factor structure. In this study, Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was performed to conduct the CFA test, ensuring the robust evaluation of the measurement model's validity for the SDGs in higher education institutions. 

(2) Statistical process control (SPC) analysis and Pareto diagrams are employed to evaluate the level of implementation of the SDGs agendas in higher education institutions using the developed measurement instrument. SPC analysis provides a systematic approach to monitor and control the implementation process, while Pareto diagrams and Importance-Performance Map analysis (IPMA) offer visual representations of the relative importance and performance of different SDGs agendas. These techniques aid in identifying areas of improvement and prioritizing resources for effective implementation. (3) Importance-Performance Map Analysis is also conducted to provide insights into the essentiality and effectiveness by the effect of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) agendas for implementation in higher education institutions. This analysis allows for the identification of SDGs agendas that are both highly important and have a significant impact on the institution's sustainability performance. It provides valuable information for strategic decision-making and resource allocation. Hence, higher education institutions can gradually implement the SDGs agendas based on their importance and effectiveness.

Title: Navigating interconnected complexities: validation and reliability of an instrument for sustainable development of education 5.0
Snippet: Abstract Sustainability actions in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) profoundly affect students, employees and their communities. These aim at social and economic benefits for local communities. Sustainability must be measured, and its goals must be achieved as part of the university’s mission to impact the community significantly. This work provides the validation results for an instrument that assesses academicians’ perceptions of HEI sustainability activities. The study began with a preliminary investigation of 121 Mexican public HEI students. The scale dimensions were constructed and validated in three steps: (a) establishing a theoretical framework to identify the necessary dimensions, (b) content validation through the judgment of five experts and (c) factor analysis and determination of instrument internal consistency to establish its reliability. The validation yielded three main findings: Aiken’s V coefficient (>0.89) showed high content-based validity indicators. Also, Cronbach’s alpha was 0.937. The exploratory factor analysis (EFA) calculated correlation coefficients for the 18-item instrument. The four variables tested in the study (economic and social impact, human rights and gender perspective, environment and work experience and social impact) yielded satisfactory internal consistency. The research affirms a methodology to measure the progress of sustainability models for Education 5.0 using technologies and resources to maximize human well-being.

The generation of knowledge through applied research (Hamadi & El-Den, 2023) contends that for the desired change in education to occur, HEIs must prioritize sustainability principles as the core foundation of their strategy ( Zal _ enien _ e & Pereira, 2021) and address the challenges of sustainability and the SDGs outlined in the 2030 agenda (Pasara, 2021). This includes incorporating these ideas into various aspects such as curricula, operations and organizational culture and empowering the institution to exert a more substantial and advantageous impact as a crucial contributor in advancing sustainability. 

Including various efforts in the university context will create a new awareness within the institution through the active participation of a wide range of stakeholders, such as students, managers, external partners, university professors and researchers. In addition, this instrument suggests interconnections with diverse SDGs by each dimension; it offers a new perspective on how they are integrated within and outside HEIs (Figure 1). Greenland et al. (2023) created a six-dimensional sustainable development model with 37 SDG aspects relating to excellent education, peace, justice and strong institutions that require sustainability training to influence stakeholder behavior. Barta et al. (2023) created an instrument with key SDG dimensions like perceptions of environmental, social, and economic compliance, organizational reputation, trust, user-organization identification and loyalty intentions to examine how an educational institution's SDG implementation affects user perceptions and loyalty, including university employees and students. Bauer et al. (2018) proposed five governance dimensions: politics, profession, organization, knowledge and visibility. Sustainable models that prioritize environmental management and enhance community relationships are essential. HEIs, while focusing on these aspects, should also recognize their role in contributing to their respective communities' economic, social and cultural development. 

Moreover, conducting validity tests ensures the reliability and accuracy of the items for each dimension, allowing for confident and contextually appropriate application within specific educational settings. The application of this assessment instrument is valuable in gauging the level of proficiency in social entrepreneurship competency at the higher education level. The final instrument, detailed in Table 7, provides universities with a means to assess their sustainability initiatives comprehensively.

documents.title: Navigating interconnected complexities: validation and reliability of an instrument for sustainable development of education 5.0
documents.snippet:
This study has important practical and research implications. HEIs must prioritize the development of a culture centered around sustainability. This involves adopting eco-friendly practices, supporting renewable energy, decreasing carbon emissions, encouraging sustainable transportation, improving energy efficiency in buildings, minimizing waste production and incorporating educational programs and curricula focusing on climate change, circular economy and corporate social responsibility. Additionally, universities should promote student-centered learning, emphasizing soft skills, ethics and awareness of social and environmental issues. It is essential to balance advanced technology and human development and assess the effectiveness of technologies that enhance teaching and learning. 

Given the scarcity of instruments that measure the maturity of sustainability in universities, especially in Mexico and Latin America, this research is particularly significant. Universities need to implement such measurements to comprehensively evaluate aspects contributing to sustainability. This instrument was developed by the Research for Challenges Group at Tecnol ogico de Monterrey and can be used by educational institutions, especially those in higher education. One challenge is establishing research institutions dedicated to advancing Education 5.0 with a focus on sustainability, as there are further ramifications associated with a technology-driven educational approach that prioritizes the welfare of humans and the environment. Furthermore, it is crucial to incorporate governance models, social innovation and public participation within ethical and sustainable principles. Another essential characteristic is developing collaboration between the community, government and corporate sectors on sustainable projects that benefit all. This collaboration enhances the connections between education and society. 

This instrument is a valuable resource for decision-makers assessing university sustainability initiatives. Further research is needed to explore whether the dimensions proposed in this instrument sufficiently address institution-specific concerns based on their contexts and locations. Additionally, incorporating political, governmental and economic aspects of the institutional development environment could enhance the instrument by including more nuanced elements from adjacent areas. 

This study aimed to report the findings of a validated instrument designed to measure the perception of the academic community regarding the sustainability activities implemented by their HEIs. After three stages, the research allowed the proposal of a four-dimensional instrument with 18 SDG-related items. With this instrument, it is possible to produce a roadmap for the pursuit of wellbeing and easily integrate actions that impact society, gaining greater trust within the academic community and among external stakeholders. The instrument's dimensions were adjusted based on the correlation findings and are displayed in Table 7.

documents.title: Developing an Instrument and Assessing SDGs Implementation in Indonesian Higher Education
documents.snippet:
The results of testing the research instrument adopted from previous studies by Aleixo et al. [2,5] and Tabucanon et al. [8] were valid and reliable in measuring the intended constructs. It has been found that all the indicators and questions in the research instrument were suitable for use. The findings indicate that the proposed measurement instrument for SDGs agendas is suitable for assessing the implementation of SDGs in higher education institutions. The instrument has been designed and tested to effectively measure the key aspects of SDGs implementation, allowing for a comprehensive assessment of progress and performance. 

By implementing this measurement instrument, higher education institutions can systematically evaluate their efforts in relation to the SDGs agendas. It provides a structured approach to assess various dimensions of sustainability development, including social, economic, and environmental aspects. The instrument allows for a comprehensive evaluation of the extent to which the institutions are aligned with and actively working towards achieving the SDGs. The instrument also facilitates benchmarking and comparisons with other institutions, fostering learning and collaboration in the pursuit of sustainable development. 

The second research objective aimed to assess the level of implementation of the 17 SDGs agendas in higher education institutions. This assessment provided valuable insights into the extent to which the SDGs agendas have been effectively implemented in these institutions. In conclusion, the findings of this study indicate that the implementation of the SDGs agendas in higher education institutions, specifically in private institutions under the Muhammadiyah organization, is positioned in the middle range. While there are notable achievements and efforts in implementing the SDGs, there is still room for improvement. 

The study reveals that certain SDGs have been prioritized and implemented with relatively good performance, while others may require further attention and strategic planning. The measurement and evaluation of tertiary institutions in Indonesia is carried out by the Higher Education Accreditation Board which is the Indonesian government's accreditation agency. Assessment indicators include nine criteria, namely vision, mission, goals and objectives; governance, governance and cooperation; student; human Resources; finance, facilities and infrastructure; education; study; community service; tridharma outcomes and achievements [36].

documents.title: Developing an Instrument and Assessing SDGs Implementation in Indonesian Higher Education
documents.snippet:
This study uses a questionnaire instrument to measure research variables. This study employs three sections of statistical techniques to comprehensively evaluate the implementation and role of higher education institutions in the sustainability agenda. 

(1) This study used SDGs measurement items referring to Aleixo et al. [2]. However, this study carefully selected and employed relevant measurement items specific to the higher education context. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) are utilized to assess the validity of the measurement items developed for evaluating the implementation of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in higher education institutions. These techniques allow for the examination of the underlying factors and the confirmation of the measurement tool's reliability and construct validity. 

EFA plays a crucial role in determining whether the selected measurement items align well with the anticipated factors, thereby indicating their suitability for effectively measuring the variable of interest. Subsequently, CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis) is utilized to validate and confirm the identified factor structure from EFA while assessing its compatibility with the collected data. CFA employs more rigorous criteria, providing formal evidence concerning the validity of the factor structure. In this study, Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was performed to conduct the CFA test, ensuring the robust evaluation of the measurement model's validity for the SDGs in higher education institutions. 

(2) Statistical process control (SPC) analysis and Pareto diagrams are employed to evaluate the level of implementation of the SDGs agendas in higher education institutions using the developed measurement instrument. SPC analysis provides a systematic approach to monitor and control the implementation process, while Pareto diagrams and Importance-Performance Map analysis (IPMA) offer visual representations of the relative importance and performance of different SDGs agendas. These techniques aid in identifying areas of improvement and prioritizing resources for effective implementation. (3) Importance-Performance Map Analysis is also conducted to provide insights into the essentiality and effectiveness by the effect of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) agendas for implementation in higher education institutions. This analysis allows for the identification of SDGs agendas that are both highly important and have a significant impact on the institution's sustainability performance. It provides valuable information for strategic decision-making and resource allocation. Hence, higher education institutions can gradually implement the SDGs agendas based on their importance and effectiveness.

documents.title: Navigating interconnected complexities: validation and reliability of an instrument for sustainable development of education 5.0
documents.snippet: Abstract Sustainability actions in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) profoundly affect students, employees and their communities. These aim at social and economic benefits for local communities. Sustainability must be measured, and its goals must be achieved as part of the university’s mission to impact the community significantly. This work provides the validation results for an instrument that assesses academicians’ perceptions of HEI sustainability activities. The study began with a preliminary investigation of 121 Mexican public HEI students. The scale dimensions were constructed and validated in three steps: (a) establishing a theoretical framework to identify the necessary dimensions, (b) content validation through the judgment of five experts and (c) factor analysis and determination of instrument internal consistency to establish its reliability. The validation yielded three main findings: Aiken’s V coefficient (>0.89) showed high content-based validity indicators. Also, Cronbach’s alpha was 0.937. The exploratory factor analysis (EFA) calculated correlation coefficients for the 18-item instrument. The four variables tested in the study (economic and social impact, human rights and gender perspective, environment and work experience and social impact) yielded satisfactory internal consistency. The research affirms a methodology to measure the progress of sustainability models for Education 5.0 using technologies and resources to maximize human well-being.
